Tiffany said that the role is a "dream come true." (Bruce Glikas/Getty Images)

"Making my Off-Broadway debut with such a funny, heartfelt and uplifting show is truly a dream come true," Tiffany said. "I’m also incredibly proud that ‘Spandex The Musical’ is partnering with Children’s Miracle Network, with a portion of the proceeds helping children and families in need."

title: Meghan Markle’s outing with Ellen DeGeneres exposes 'irony' in royal’s ‘quiet country life’: expert
summary: Meghan Markle's first photographed outing in the Cotswolds with Ellen DeGeneres and Portia de Rossi raises questions about her quiet life claims.
story: Kinsey Schofield, host of YouTube's "Kinsey Schofield Unfiltered," argues Prince Harry and Meghan Markle choose publicity while seeking privacy and says their royal status should be made clear.
Meghan Markle is raising questions after being photographed in England with two Hollywood stars.

The 45-year-old royal was recently photographed in the Cotswolds with Ellen DeGeneres and her wife, Portia de Rossi, in her first photographed outing since arriving in the U.K., which Kinsey Schofield, host of YouTube’s "Kinsey Schofield Unfiltered" said hints that "there is already going to be considerably less privacy for Meghan in Britain than perhaps she anticipated."

"But there is an irony here too. If Harry and Meghan genuinely wanted to disappear into quiet country life, the Cotswolds is one of the places where they could probably accomplish that," Schofield told Fox News Digital. "Instead, Meghan’s first photographed social outing is with Ellen DeGeneres and Portia de Rossi. That tells me she remains very interested in celebrity and in being associated with recognizable, high-profile people."

Schofield added that she finds it "interesting" that Markle "appears to have changed countries without necessarily changing the social ecosystem she prefers," noting that when living in Montecito, she and Prince Harry were spending time with "wealthy, famous and influential people."
Markle was photographed with Ellen DeGeneres and Portia de Rossi in her first public outing since moving back to England. (Harold Cunningham/Getty Images)
PRINCE HARRY, MEGHAN MARKLE ACCUSED OF SEEKING ‘BEST OF BOTH WORLDS’ WITH UK MOVE: EXPERT

The idea that her first photographed outing since moving to the U.K. was with "two fellow American celebrity transplants" isn't "inherently wrong" in Schofield's eyes, but she argues that it challenges the "idea that Meghan has returned to Britain simply to embrace a quieter, more anonymous country life."
"If anything, this suggests she may be trying to recreate elements of Montecito in the Cotswolds: privacy when she wants it, but with a glamorous and recognizable social circle around her," she said.

Schofield also noted that Markle's behavior, in comparison to Prince Harry's, also highlights her interest "in commercial and monetary opportunities," while showing he is "determined to maintain the appearance and rhythm of royal life."

"Harry likes the engagements, the causes, the speeches and the sense of public duty," she said. "Meghan seems happier pursuing celebrity and commercial opportunities. title: Ed Sheeran concertgoers warn artists about sharing political views: 'You're going to alienate' fans
summary: Ed Sheeran fans at his Philadelphia concert warned artists that political statements alienate audiences. Sheeran's Gillette Stadium shows, planned for the weekend, were canceled due to weather.
story: The "Shape of You" singer held a solo concert last weekend in Philadelphia after Macklemore was dropped from the tour over his pro-Palestinian comments.

Several fans who attended Ed Sheeran’s concert in Philadelphia last weekend after Macklemore was dropped for making "Free Palestine" comments, warned other artists that if they make political statements, they will alienate half of their audience.

The "Bad Habits" singer was expected to play his second and third concerts since the controversy this Friday and Saturday at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts, which is owned by Robert Kraft.
However, both shows have since been canceled.

"Due to the severe weather warnings in place in Boston and across New England throughout the weekend and following consultation with local officials, we have made the difficult decision to cancel the Ed Sheeran concerts at Gillette Stadium," tour promoter Messina Touring said in a statement on Friday. "The decision was made with the safety of fans, staff and everyone involved in the shows as the top priority."
ROBERT KRAFT, GILLETTE STADIUM BOOT MACKLEMORE FROM ED SHEERAN TOUR OVER ‘FREE PALESTINE’ RANT
Ed Sheeran is seen performing at a concert in December. (Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for iHeartRadio)
Previously, the New England Patriots owner allegedly threatened to cancel the concerts at his venue if Macklemore wasn’t taken off the tour, according to the "Thrift Shop" rapper.
Macklemore also claimed Kraft got other stadium owners to agree to not allow Sheeran to play at their venues if the rapper was still with his tour.

"The fact that they’re forcing Ed Sheeran to have an opinion is not right," one woman told Fox News Digital outside last Saturday’s concert. "He wants to stay in the middle – if you have an opinion, that’s fine, but you’re going to alienate at least 50% of your population, and it causes unrest."
GOO GOO DOLLS' JOHN RZEZNIK DRAWS LINE ON POLITICS AT CONCERTS: 'I'M NOT GOING TO LECTURE YOU'

She said the "Shape of You" singer "just wants to do his music and play his music, and people want to enjoy it. They want to get away from it, and I don’t feel as though they should have to worry about this stuff when they come to a concert."

Macklemore was dropped as the opening act for Sheeran’s tour earlier this month after he made pro-Palestinian comments at two concerts. The other supporting acts on Sheeran’s tour quit in solidarity with Macklemore.
WATCH: ED SHEERAN CONCERTGOERS WEIGH IN ON MUSICIANS MAKING POLITICAL STATEMENTS
LIBERAL LAWMAKERS, ACTIVISTS RALLY BEHIND MACKLEMORE AFTER SHEERAN TOUR REMOVAL OVER 'FREE PALESTINE' STANCE

In Philadelphia Saturday night, Sheeran made a nearly four-minute-long speech in which he explained to fans that he never wanted to be an activist musician and that he was there continuing his tour alone because he wanted to honor his commitment to fans.
Macklemore performs at a concert at the end of August. (AFP via Getty Images)
ED SHEERAN FACES GROWING BACKLASH AS RADIO STATION BANS SONGS, PROTEST GROUPS RESPOND TO MACKLEMORE'S REMOVAL
He said he can also see both sides of such a complex issue, admitting that he doesn’t know enough about it, is still learning and will make mistakes as he tries to navigate the situation.

He added that he could no longer hide how he feels about the humanitarian issue.

Another fan told Fox News Digital ahead of the concert last Saturday that, as artists and musicians have a right to speak their minds: "They also don’t have to — they’re entertainment. I have a right to choose to listen or to not listen. I think it’s all about my choice — I live in America, I can decide to ignore or to listen, and they have the same right."
Fans arrive for Ed Sheeran's concert at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia on Sept. 19. (AFP via Getty Images)
GORILLAZ FRONTMAN DAMON ALBARN HOLDS UP PALESTINIAN FLAG DURING SHOW AFTER MACKLEMORE TOUR REMOVAL

"It’s a really tough thing," a woman, who told Fox News Digital she is a schoolteacher, said outside the concert. "I am in a classroom every day, and I have my own thoughts on politics in the same way that I’m sure every artist does. I also do not share those with my students because I want them to have a safe space where they are who they are, and I think that’s kind of the same way I want concerts to be. I want us to have a space where we can be happy and get away from the rest of the world for a little while, and that’s why we’re here."

Another woman at the concert noted that musicians like Sheeran are just trying to make a living.

"I support the artists — they’re here for the right reasons, and they’re here to make a living, they’re doing something that they love, and they pursue their music for a reason," she told Fox News Digital. title: Roseanne Barr calls former co-star a 'brainwashed bigot' after he said reboot was 'rightfully canceled'
summary: Roseanne Barr called Michael Fishman a "brainwashed bigot" on a podcast after he said the 2018 "Roseanne" hit reboot was "rightfully canceled."
story: Roseanne Barr told Fox News Digital she believes her upbringing was the perfect depiction of the American experience.
Roseanne Barr is firing back at her former co-star, calling him a "brainwashed bigot."

During a recent appearance on the "Can't Be Censored" podcast, the 73-year-old actress and comedian hit back at her former "Roseanne" co-star, Michael Fishman, after he said the 2018 reboot was "rightfully canceled."

"He f---ing doesn’t even f---ing know what I said, even though I’ve explained it 10,000 times for nine years on the internet," Barr said. "He hasn’t even taken the time to listen to what I say because he’s a bigot. And he’s a brainwashed bigot."

The reboot of the hit '90s show was a huge success when it premiered in March 2018 but was canceled just two months later after Barr tweeted a racist remark about Valerie Jarrett, a former advisor to former President Obama.
Barr fired back at her former co-star who said ABC was right to cancel the "Roseanne" reboot. (Getty Images)
ROSEANNE BARR REVEALS ‘DAMAGED’ HEART, FEARS SHE WILL ‘DIE ON THE SURGERY TABLE’

Barr apologized for the remark multiple times. However, ABC decided to fire her and cancel the show. A month later, the network announced a new spin-off called "The Connors," bringing back a majority of the "Roseanne" cast without any involvement from Barr.
The comedian went on to say that Fishman asked her about her comments "9,000" times before she told him to "go and f--- yourself and stay f---ed ‘till the day you die."

"Don’t put my name in your f---ng mouth; shut the f--- up," she recalled telling him. "You are an ignoramus and a bigot, and you have no idea what I said because it contradicts the Democratic Party platform that you’ve had shoved down your throat and up your a--. So, just f--- you. You have no geopolitical context whatsoever to discuss what I said."
Fishman fired back after Barr reignited their years-old feud, but the former child star appeared to take a different approach to the comedian’s blistering comments.

"I know everybody wants a response to Roseanne’s comments," Fishman said in a statement shared on social media, before taking a moment to thank Barr for acknowledging that he did reach out to her after her 2018 controversy.
Michael Fishman and Roseanne Barr appear in a 1990 episode of "Roseanne." (ABC Photo Archives / Getty Images)

Fishman continued to explain that he showed Barr "compassion" during her scandal, even though he "vehemently disagreed" with her. He said that her memory of how she responded to his attempts to discuss the issue was accurate, and that he'd kept the things she said to him to himself "for her protection."

"But I guess she gave you a glimpse into the darker side of my childhood," he admitted, before adding that he does have "tremendous gratitude" for the time he spent working with her on the original show.

The actor, who played D.J. Conner on "Roseanne," also reflected on the complicated nature of their relationship, saying, "I’m living something publicly that a lot of you have been navigating privately," referring to the experience of "caring and loving someone who’s been a powerful part of your life and who’s changed and we don’t understand. And we don’t agree with it."

Despite the fallout, Fishman said he plans to respond with compassion rather than anger. "I’m going to choose to remember the best in them, and I’m also going to set some healthy boundaries for myself," he said. "We get to decide who we are, and our actions show who we are." He concluded his statement by saying, "I’m going to make art from the joy and the pain."
Metcalf said she hasn't spoken to Barr since they finished filming the reboot. (Adam Rose/Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)
In a recent interview with The New Yorker, Laurie Metcalf, who played Barr's sister, Jackie Harris, on the show, said the two "haven’t spoken since we said goodbye at the end of the reboot."
Barr confirmed she has not kept in touch with any of her former co-stars during an interview with Fox News Digital in June 2025.

"No, I'm not friends with none of them. They're all in the past," she said. "I have pleasant memories of what fun we had, wish them all the best. And, no, we don't talk. I've moved on from that horrendous ending and chapter of my life, but you know, I don't hold any bitterness or nothing to them. But, my God, what fun we had on that show.

title: Dolly Parton’s sisters push back on feud rumors after nephew’s legal battle with star's estate erupts
summary: Dolly Parton's sisters deny family feud claims after manager Danny Nozell won a restraining order against nephew Bryan Seaver over alleged threats.
story: Entertainment lawyer Jordan Matthews weighs in on the conflict involving Dolly Parton’s nephew and explains why disputes among relatives can intensify when a famous person leaves behind a valuable brand.
Dolly Parton’s sisters are shutting down claims of a family feud as tensions surrounding the late country legend’s legacy have spilled into court.

Nearly one month after Parton’s death, her sisters pushed back against reports of infighting within the family, insisting they remain united as a separate legal dispute involving the singer’s longtime manager and nephew resulted in a temporary restraining order.

"I’ll say this and this only: there is no feud within our family," Freida Parton shared Wednesday on Instagram. "No one among the Parton/Owens family is fighting over Dolly’s estate. We all love Bryan, just as we all love each other. I love you all!!"
DOLLY PARTON’S SISTER REVEALS ‘LAST THING’ COUNTRY LEGEND ASKED OF HER BEFORE DEATH
Dolly Parton’s sisters, Freida Parton and Stella Parton, pushed back against reports of a family feud following the singer's death. (Ron Galella/Ron Galella Collection)
Parton's sister Stella echoed Freida's message, emphasizing that the family remains united as it continues to navigate its grief.
"It has been a comfort to experience such an outpouring of love on [Dolly's] behalf as we grieve her passing," Stella posted Thursday on Instagram.
"We are also grieving the loss of our brother Denver who passed less than a month before her. All families have the same struggles since we are all living in this world having a human experience!
"We are still intact and moving forward because our children and grandchildren look to us for strength and guidance during this difficult time of loss and confusion for them as well," she added.

"Regardless of what you may have seen on different news outlets, we are all doing what you would be doing under the same circumstances, we are living our lives one day at a time and being grateful for every blessing."

Parton’s legacy took a dramatic turn this week when her longtime manager sought a restraining order against the country icon’s nephew.

Danny Nozell, who runs She's Alive, LLC, an entity Parton created to oversee her business interests, filed for the restraining order on behalf of She's Alive against Bryan Seaver and Seaver's private security company, Squadron Augmented Protection Services, in Nashville, according to The Associated Press.

A Tennessee judge granted the temporary restraining order Wednesday, citing a pattern of alleged threats and demands for payment, along with Seaver’s "claimed access to weapons, experience with violence, and intention to retaliate." story: Mike 'Gunz' Gunzelman discusses the backlash surrounding Ed Sheeran's tour after opening acts quit in support of Macklemore.
Macklemore is taking his views on "Free Palestine" on the road.

The rapper, who was dropped from Ed Sheeran's tour earlier this month after stirring controversy with his politically charged performances, announced Thursday that he's going on a new tour he's calling the "Free Palestine Tour."

"If these last couple of weeks have shown us anything, it’s that something has shifted over the last three years. There has been a collective awakening around Palestinian liberation, the power of billionaires that try to censor that call, and what we expect from artists right now," he wrote on Instagram.

Macklemore wrote that "what happened to me is bigger than one artist or one stage," and that "when the billionaire class can decide which voices are allowed on stage and which ones are too dangerous to hear, everyone should be paying attention."
He added, "So, as you all know, my schedule freed up a bit."

He wrote that for the past week, he's been in touch with artists who have also been vocal about their support for Palestinians, "regardless of the consequences" — artists who he says "understand that our platforms mean very little if we’re only willing to use them when it’s safe."

title: David Charvet admits he walked away from Hollywood after 'Baywatch' to focus on fatherhood
summary: David Charvet reveals why he left Hollywood over a decade ago and how "Special Forces: World's Toughest Test" let him prove something to his kids.
story: The former "Baywatch" star called his children his "legacy" and said he participated in "Special Forces" to show his children what he gave up for them.
David Charvet is opening up about why he left Hollywood.
In a new interview with Fox News Digital, the 54-year-old actor discussed his experience on Fox's hit series, "Special Forces: World's Toughest Test," and why he stepped away from Hollywood in 2013.

"I left Hollywood because I wanted to be a good dad, and for me, today my children are my legacy," he said. "It's not the career you built or the money you have or all that. It's really what you leave behind. And what I'm leaving one day behind is really my children. And if I did it right in that way, then I think I've successfully done my job as a man on this planet. So, for me, there's no regrets."
Having left Hollywood over a decade ago, Charvet expressed how "honored" he is "to be amongst all these people and just to be a part of it."
Charvet quit acting in order to be a good father to his two kids, who he shares with his ex-wife, Brooke Burke. (Kim Raff/Getty Images for Operation Smile)
‘SPECIAL FORCES’ STARS JESSIE JAMES DECKER, HUSBAND ERIC SHARE KEY TO SUCCESSFUL 12-YEAR MARRIAGE
The actor became famous playing lifeguard Matt Brody on "Baywatch," saying no one told him that he "was going to be a 'Baywatch' guy forever," but he doesn't mind.

"That's where I got my start. The show was incredible, it reached everywhere around the world," he said. "I've had a lot of incredible opportunities from it. Incredible life lessons, incredible friendships and relationships, so for me, I'm just grateful, you know, I'm super happy with whatever the outcome has been."
WATCH: David Charvet admits he left Hollywood in order to be a good dad to his two kids
The original "Baywatch" helped launch not only Charvet's career, but also put Pamela Anderson, Carmen Electra and many of its other stars on the map.

It was announced in September 2025 that a reboot of the series starring a whole new batch of lifeguards was in the works. In addition to seasoned actors, including Stephen Amel and Shay Mitchell, the show is also a launching pad for acting newcomers, Brooks Nader, Livvy Dunne and Noah Beck.
Charvet starred as Matt Brody in "Baywatch." (Ron Galella, Ltd./Ron Galella Collection via Getty Images)

"I got to say that what we created 25 years ago was very special. At the same time, there was only 14 channels at the time. So people got a chance to see that show more probably today than what people are going to see in the next season that's about to come," he said about the new series. "Our executive producers, which are, I believe, executive producers today, were real lifeguards, live the life as lifeguards, so there were real stories."

'BAYWATCH' STAR BROOKS NADER'S CONSERVATIVE PARENTS BANNED BIKINIS GROWING UP AS SHE SLIPS INTO RED SWIMSUIT

Charvet is excited to see what the new generation brings to the show, but admits, "getting people to really watch something today is more of a challenge," and says the writers have to be "more creative" now than before, adding, "They got their work cut out for them."
While he was considered a big star in his heyday, Charvet has "been out of the game" for over 20 years, and admits his "kids have never seen me on television or in movies or anything live."

He explained to Fox News Digital that that was part of the reason he agreed to compete on the show, noting it "was really important for me to maybe show them that aspect of what I kind of gave up for them." He shares two children with his ex-wife, Brooke Burke; a daughter, Rain and a son, Shaya.

To take on what we took on was a real thing that I wanted to see if I could do. So for me, it was a huge challenge, an incredible opportunity, and hopefully my kids will be proud."

title: ‘Rocky IV’ star Dolph Lundgren says he planned his own funeral during brutal cancer battle
summary: Dolph Lundgren reveals in his new memoir "Fights Worth Fighting" that he planned his own funeral during his nearly decade-long cancer battle.
story: Actor Dolph Lundgren joins Fox & Friends to discuss his new memoir ‘Fights Worth Fighting,’ his journey to Hollywood and his battle with cancer.
This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or 1-800-273-TALK (8255).
Dolph Lundgren was preparing to die.

The Swedish actor, who famously played Soviet boxer Ivan Drago in "Rocky IV," has written a new memoir, "Fights Worth Fighting: Finding Strength in Struggle." In it, the 68-year-old details his grueling journey with cancer.
‘ROCKY’ STAR DOLPH LUNDGREN SWEARS BY THIS SECRET FOR STRONG MARRIAGE
Fox News may be compensated for or earn a commission if you buy through our referral links.
"Fights Worth Fighting: Finding Strength in Struggle" by Dolph Lundgren is available now. (Harper Horizon)
The star was diagnosed in 2015 after doctors found a cancerous tumor in his kidney. Lundgren had surgery to remove the tumor and continued appearing in movies like "Creed II" and "Aquaman."
After remaining cancer-free for five years, doctors discovered more tumors in 2020. He later learned the cancer had spread to his liver, both lungs, spine and in and around his left kidney.
Dolph Lundgren opened up about the dark moments in his cancer journey. (© Per Bernal)

"I had a lot of difficult conversations with myself," Lundgren told Fox News Digital. "I definitely had a few tough ones. Of course, as most older men do, you do estate planning. You plan your will and who's going to get what. But in this case, it was around the corner. It was something I had to plan a little more in detail, like funerals and trying to figure out where I would be, what would be better for my family. Planning your own funeral is kind of a saying, but I literally was doing that. That was tough."
WATCH: DOLPH LUNDGREN OPENS UP ABOUT CANCER BATTLE, BECOMING US CITIZEN IN ‘FIGHTS WORTH FIGHTING’
During that time, Lundgren said he considered ending his life.

"At some point, which was even harder, I started thinking, 'Do I really want to be in bed weighing 60 pounds and having people come and see me like that? Or should I just end it myself?'" Lundgren said. "I started considering that. I spoke to my brother. We made a deal, and he would help me out if it came to that, if I made that decision. But it was a tough conversation."
Swedish actor Dolph Lundgren with American actor, director and screenwriter Sylvester Stallone on the set of his movie "Rocky IV." (Sunset Boulevard/Corbis via Getty Images)

In the book, Lundgren wrote, "When I was deep into the cancer treatments and thinking about the possibility of killing myself, my brother, Johan, was going to help me, because I didn’t know what kind of condition I might be in once I made that decision. I could be in really bad shape by then and not capable of completing the suicide on my own."
Dolph Lundgren was diagnosed with kidney cancer in 2015. (Emma Krokdal)

"There are countries in Europe, like Switzerland, that permit legal suicide for people who are terminally ill, but I still might have needed someone there to help me," he continued. "Johan and I talked about it, but once I met Dr. Drakaki and began feeling a little better, it never went any further than that."
Lundgren’s longtime friend Johan Pramell also said in the memoir that the star "wanted to go out in glory like a Viking because he didn't want people to have to watch him suffer or fade away."
Dolph with his first wife, Anette, and daughters, Ida and Greta, on a family vacation. (Author's private collection)

Medical aid in dying is not synonymous with euthanasia, according to the Online Journal of Issues in Nursing. The journal states that laws allowing medical aid in dying permit eligible adults with terminal illnesses to self-administer medication when certain criteria are met.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Dolph Lundgren and his cat, Bello, on his birthday. (Emma Krokdal)
Euthanasia, which is not legal in the United States, occurs when someone other than the patient administers medication with the intent of hastening the patient’s death, the journal states.
According to Dignity in Dying, a U.K.-based advocacy organization, 10 countries in Europe have laws that allow people experiencing "unbearable suffering" to access assisted dying.
Dolph Lundgren told Fox News Digital he wrote his memoir in hopes it will inspire others to keep fighting. (Emma Krokdal)
But one thing was certain — Lundgren wasn't ready to die.
Dolph Lundgren is seen here throwing a punch during treatment. (Emma Krokdal)

"I have a certain discipline, a fighter's heart, since I was a kid," he told Fox News Digital. "I think that was helpful. I may have had these thoughts, but the other side of me wants to go another round to see what happens. Maybe the other guy will drop. You never know. I think that's a part of it."

"But also, I believe being in good physical shape helped me, and continuing to work out through the whole thing," he said. "As much as I could, I would stay physically active. And then I was lucky to have my wife, who was very supportive, and my daughters."
A second opinion changed everything for Dolph Lundgren in his quest to be cancer-free. (Daniele Venturelli/Daniele Venturelli/Getty Images)
"They're the ones that kept me going by just their sheer presence," he added.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Dolph Lundgren and his wife are seen here in Greece. (Author's private collection)

At one point, a doctor in the U.K. told Lundgren he likely had two or three years left to live. Lundgren wrote in his memoir that he believed, based on the doctor's tone, his prognosis could have been closer to one or two years.

After returning to Los Angeles, Lundgren sought a second opinion from Dr. Alexandra Drakaki, an oncologist at UCLA Health, whom he credited with saving his life. "At this point, I was depressed and had almost given up all hope," he wrote.
Dolph Lundgren poses for photographers at the Jameson Empire Film Awards held at the Grosvenor House Hotel, Park Lane, in London on March 25, 2012. (Carl Cour/AFP via Getty Images)
According to the memoir, Drakaki determined that his cancer had been misdiagnosed, leading to a different treatment approach.
"What she found was that my 'kidney cancer' cells had a mutation that is fairly common in lung cancer," he wrote. "That's why the medications I had been given for the past two years weren't working."
Dolph Lundgren is seen here becoming a U.S. citizen in 2024. (Emma Krokdal)
After Lundgren went public with his cancer battle, one heavyweight stood in his corner: Sylvester Stallone.

"Stallone and I have a long history, a good, long relationship together," he said. "We've known each other for 40 years. We've made six films together over that period. He went from being a mentor, a boss on set, director, producer. I was just a new kid on the block. And then slowly, we moved together and became more equals, I would say, two older guys who've been in the business a long time. And he has three daughters, I have two, and we share that as well."
Dolph Lundgren is seen here training at a martial arts camp. (Author's private collection)

"When I got sick, he reached out to me," Lundgren said. "It was unexpected because he was the first one, actually, who reached out of everybody, even before some of my family, when it came out. And he was very emotional about it. It touched me. And that was another side of him that I'd never seen. Since then, we've been very close friends, even closer than before."

In November 2024, Lundgren announced he was cancer-free. In his memoir, he reflects on whether performance-enhancing drugs may have played a role in his cancer battle.

Lundgren wrote that he used anabolic steroids and other performance-enhancing drugs on and off from 1986 to 1996 while preparing for physically demanding movie roles. While he stressed that there is "no conclusive evidence" the drugs caused his cancer, he acknowledged they "might have helped cause" it, adding that he could not say for certain.
Dolph Lundgren with daughters Ida Lundgren, left, and Greta Lundgren attending the "Aquaman" premiere held at Cineworld in Leicester Square, London. (Ian West/PA Images via Getty Images)

"I wanted to be candid about my past and what I've been through," Lundgren explained. "And I think nobody knows what steroids and other performance-enhancing drugs do to us. The data is not conclusive. And I always thought it could not help me in my medical situation. I wanted to express a caution to people, to other young men, who may decide to try it, that it's not without risk."
Dolph Lundgren is seen in New York City on Sept. 22, 2026. (GC Images)

"I try to forgive and let go of everything from my past," he said. "That's very important to me. So, I don't blame myself. I was younger. I wasn't as smart as I am now. And I had pressures from the business. Is it really good for you? I doubt it. I really do."
Now, Lundgren said he still has plenty of fight in him.

Dolph Lundgren attends a photocall on June 22, 2024, in Santa Margherita di Pula, Italy. (Daniele Venturelli/Daniele Venturelli/Getty Images)

"I've obviously touched a lot of people as an actor in my business, and that's good," he said. "I've brightened up people's lives. I think that's great. That makes me feel good. I now hope to offer a little inspiration to others. I know I have so much more I want to do."

title: Dolly Parton’s legacy battle escalates as manager granted restraining order against star's nephew
summary: Danny Nozell's restraining order request against Bryan Seaver revealed alleged threats to destroy Dolly Parton's brand partnerships after her death.
story: Fox News contributor Billy Bush breaks down the court battle emerging between the singer’s nephew and her manager on ‘The Story.’
A bitter battle over Dolly Parton’s legacy took a dramatic turn when her longtime manager sought a restraining order against the country icon’s nephew.

Danny Nozell, who runs She's Alive, LLC, an entity Parton created to oversee her business interests, filed for a restraining order against Bryan Seaver in Nashville, according to The Associated Press.

A Tennessee judge granted the temporary restraining order Wednesday, citing a pattern of alleged threats and demands for payment, along with Seaver’s "claimed access to weapons, experience with violence, and intention to retaliate." The order called the communications "concerning" and specifically pointed to an alleged threat to use force.

The order barred Seaver and his company, Squadron Augmented Protection Services, which provided Parton’s security detail, from entering She’s Alive properties or coming within 1,000 feet of its employees and business partners. It also prohibited Seaver from contacting them.
DOLLY PARTON'S LIFE IN HER OWN WORDS: FROM SMOKY MOUNTAINS POVERTY TO COUNTRY MUSIC IMMORTALITY
Dolly Parton’s longtime manager, Danny Nozell, filed for a restraining order against Dolly Parton’s nephew, Bryan Seaver, after alleged threatening messages. (Katherine Bomboy/NBC via Getty Images)
Parton chose Seaver to publicly announce her death. The singer-songwriter died Aug. 25. Less than a month later, a behind-the-scenes feud erupted into a legal battle.

Nozell and She's Alive accused Seaver of sending increasingly threatening messages in the weeks leading up to their request for a temporary restraining order. The filing came after She’s Alive fired Seaver over his alleged "terrorizing conduct."
Court documents obtained by The Associated Press show text messages and emails allegedly sent by Seaver.
The messages initially included threats to destroy the brand and, after Parton’s death, allegedly showed Seaver reveling in his newfound fame and calling himself an "international arms dealer."

According to the court documents, the alleged messages rattled those within Parton’s business circle, leading several employees to resign and her trust and estate attorney to step away. She’s Alive also brought in private security to protect employees at work and at their homes.
She's Alive terminated Seaver Sept. 15 and asked the court to bar Parton's nephew from contacting or coming within 1,000 feet of its employees, attorneys and business partners.

title: Harvey Weinstein sentenced to 15 years in prison for 2006 sex crime in New York
summary: Harvey Weinstein apologized while maintaining his innocence, and a Manhattan judge called him a sexual predator and the face of the #MeToo movement.
story: Harvey Weinstein was sentenced to 15 years in prison after being convicted in a New York retrial of sexually assaulting former TV production assistant Miriam Haley at his Manhattan apartment in 2006.
Harvey Weinstein, the disgraced movie mogul, was sentenced in Manhattan to 15 years in prison Wednesday for a felony sex crime in another #MeToo reckoning.

Weinstein’s sentencing for sexually assaulting one-time TV production assistant Miriam Haley followed a legal odyssey spanning more than six years. His 2020 conviction was overturned by New York's highest court. A second jury found Weinstein guilty again at a retrial last year.

Once among the most powerful figures in the entertainment industry, Weinstein was an Oscar-winning producer whose hits included "Shakespeare in Love," "Pulp Fiction" and "Chocolat." But his downfall came quickly after sexual assault allegations in 2017 set off the #MeToo movement.

Weinstein, 74, is expected to appeal and maintains that he never raped or sexually assaulted anyone. He is now likely to remain behind bars well into his 80s. Seated in a wheelchair, he was quickly moved out of the courtroom after the sentencing, while some of his accusers hugged and brushed away tears.
JONATHAN TURLEY: WHEN JOURNALISTS WHINE ABOUT #METOO, THEY DON’T MEAN PLATNER, TOO
Harvey Weinstein was sentenced to 15 years in prison in Manhattan after his conviction for sexually assaulting Miriam Haley. (Dean Moses/amNewYork via AP, Pool)
Weinstein and his victim both spoke in court

Weinstein faced up to 25 years in prison for sexually assaulting Haley at his Manhattan apartment in 2006. He has already served more than six years as his case cycled through the criminal justice system. Haley gave her account of the assault at two trials and again addressed the court Wednesday.

"Having been sexually assaulted by Harvey Weinstein has had a devastating effect on my life and sense of security that may never go away. Making the decision to speak up will have me looking over my shoulder for years to come," Haley said.
"It’s a life sentence for me."
Minutes later, Weinstein apologized while reiterating his innocence.

"Reflecting on all that has happened since 2017 has helped me recognize how my past conduct has negatively affected others. I live with many regrets and sincerely apologize to anyone I have affected with my actions," he said.
EX-MAYOR FOUND LIABLE FOR ALLEGED SEXUAL ASSAULTS OF 7 WOMEN, ORDERED TO PAY $13M
Harvey Weinstein, 74, was sentenced Wednesday to 15 years in prison for sexually assaulting former TV production assistant Miriam Haley. (AP Photo/Michael Sisak)
Some of his accusers who were in court shook their heads while he spoke.
Judge Curtis Farber said Weinstein was once a king in the movie industry, "but recognition for these achievements will pale in comparison to what you did."
He said Weinstein is now known as "a sexual predator, the literal face of the #MeToo movement."
The judge said Weinstein treated women as "mere objects to be played with and discarded" and still hasn’t accepted responsibility, portraying himself as a victim during jailhouse interviews.
Haley afterward said she was happy with the sentence, while saying it's clear that Weinstein has not acknowledged what he did.
"I think he still feels entitled, and that’s part of the problem," she said.
ARMIE HAMMER COMPARES HIS HOLLYWOOD EXILE TO BEING CRUCIFIED: 'THE NAILS ARE IN MY HANDS'
Harvey Weinstein received a 15-year prison sentence after a retrial again found him guilty of sexually assaulting Miriam Haley. (AP Photo/Michael Sisak)
Haley’s lawyer, the famed victims’ rights attorney Gloria Allred, rejected any suggestion that Weinstein’s sentencing means the #MeToo era is over.
"Women are empowered in a way they have never been before," she said.
Weinstein was originally sentenced to 23 years in prison after a jury convicted him of assaulting Haley and raping an aspiring actress, Jessica Mann, in 2013.

Tried for a second time last year, he was again convicted of a first-degree criminal sex act for assaulting Haley, who has also gone by the name Mimi Haleyi. In a messy split verdict, the jury acquitted him of forcibly performing oral sex on another woman, Kaja Sokola, and could not reach a verdict on a rape charge involving Mann.
After another retrial ended in a hung jury in May, Manhattan prosecutors dropped the rape charge rather than pursue a fourth trial after Mann said she could not bear to testify again.
Weinstein’s health issues pushed the defense to ask for leniency.
SETH ROGEN REFUSES TO OFFER JAMES FRANCO A SECOND CHANCE AFTER SEXUAL MISCONDUCT CLAIMS
Harvey Weinstein was sentenced to 15 years in prison after a yearslong legal battle that included the reversal of his 2020 conviction. (Steven Hirsch/New York Post via AP, Pool)
Defense lawyer Jacob Kaplan wanted three more years on top of the six years Weinstein already served, saying a longer sentence would make it more likely that Weinstein dies in prison.
Weinstein has been in the hospital six times since 2025, Kaplan said, while dealing with blood cancer, congestive heart failure and kidney issues.

Weinstein is also awaiting resentencing in a separate rape case in Los Angeles. A California appeals court upheld the 2022 conviction but threw out his original 16-year sentence because the judge had considered his New York convictions — that were later thrown out — as an aggravating factor.

After shuffling between state prison, where he tested positive for COVID-19 early in the pandemic, and New York City’s notorious Rikers Island complex, Weinstein has been housed at a medical unit for inmates at Bellevue Hospital in Manhattan.
Haley, 49, is a former entertainment producer now working in advertising.
She said she met Weinstein through a mutual connection and worked briefly as a production assistant on "Project Runway," a reality competition show that he produced.
FOUR MORE WOMEN ACCUSE FORMER NFL PLAYER OF SEXUAL ASSAULT AMID EXISTING ALLEGATIONS: 'BLATANT LIES'
Harvey Weinstein maintained his innocence and apologized to people affected by his past conduct before a judge sentenced him to 15 years in prison. (Steven Hirsch/New York Post via AP, Pool)

Haley said she accepted an invitation to visit Weinstein’s apartment, and, after chatting briefly, he lunged to kiss her, she testified. She said she rebuffed him, but he grabbed her, forcibly backed her into a bedroom and sexually assaulted her, ignoring her pleas to stop.
She recalled Weinstein asking, "Don’t you think we’re much closer now?" after either the alleged assault or a subsequent occasion when she says she had unwanted, but not forced, sex with him.
She also recalled telling him after the second encounter, "You know you can’t keep doing this."

title: Judge Judy says those who don't like America should 'go somewhere else'
summary: Judge Judy doubles down on her love of America, praising capitalism and personal responsibility. The TV icon also addresses 1950s nostalgia and a longing for law and order.
story: Fran Weinstein shares how Judge Judy responded to a matchmaking request with a bold take on independence. The retired "Entertainment Tonight" producer has written a memoir, "Tortured Soles."
Judge Judy is doubling down on her love of America, telling people who want to fundamentally change the country to "go somewhere else."
During an interview with USA Today, Judy Sheindlin, 83, opened up about her views on America and the enduring popularity of her courtroom television persona.
"I have a house, and I have a home. I consider America my home. America has been good to me. I think that it’s the greatest country in the world," Sheindlin said.
JUDGE JUDY PREPARING TO END DECADES-LONG RUN AS TV'S TOUGHEST JUDGE
Judge Judy tells America's critics to "go somewhere else." (Getty Images for Keep Memory Alive)

"If you don’t like this country, go somewhere else," she continued. "Don’t come to the greatest country in the world, the most successful country in the world, and say, ‘I want to change it.’ There are other countries that are the something else that you want. Go there. Go there. But don’t come into my home and say, ‘I want to change it.’"
"We are a capitalist country that revered excellence, that revered entrepreneurship, that revered all the things that made us great," she added. "Whether you like it or not, it's there."
Sheindlin’s comments came as CBS celebrated the 30th anniversary of "Judge Judy" with the primetime special "Judge Judy: Unfiltered, Unforgettable."

The TV icon also addressed the growing nostalgia for an earlier era, suggesting that many people are craving elements of the 1950s — including a greater sense of order, personal responsibility and common decency.

Judge Judy Sheindlin appears on the set of her television show in Los Angeles on Dec. 2, 1997. (Bob Riha Jr./Getty Images)

"You can't pick up a paper without seeing violence and hate speech and antisemitism and racism and cruelty and beheadings," she continues. "People can't even get together with their families anymore, because you have one section of the family that is more liberal, one is more conservative. They can't even talk to each other with civility."

"People are frustrated in the same way they were 30 years ago," she recently told W Magazine. "They like rules, law, order, and personal responsibility."
Judge Judy Sheindlin said she plans to step away from the camera after decades in the industry.  (Lloyd Bishop/NBCU Photo Bank/NBCUniversal)

"They like their neighbors to be nice and quiet, to keep their cats on their own property," she added. "There are reasons for bad behavior, but there are never excuses for bad behavior if it affects someone else."

title: Presley Gerber’s final hours at rehab in focus amid cause of death questions
summary: Presley Gerber's final hours draws questions. Police are investigating the 27-year-old model's death as a suspected overdose.
story: Presley Gerber, model and son of Cindy Crawford, has died at the age of 27. TMZ executive producer Michael Babcock discusses the investigation into Gerber's death and his past struggles with mental health and substance abuse.
Presley Gerber died Sunday, Sept. 20 – one day after entering the Resolutions Living rehabilitation facility in Santa Monica, Calif. He was 27.

Based off Wilshire Boulevard in an affluent Southern California community, the center is described as a co-ed home which "provides the structure" for residents on their journey to recovery from mental health, addiction, and co-occurring disorders through intensive outpatient programs of their choosing.

While it remained unclear why Cindy Crawford's son entered the center or what treatment he was receiving, wrongful death and personal injury attorney John J. Perlstein warned against jumping to conclusions of liability as the investigation continued into Gerber's death.
PRESLEY GERBER'S DEATH BEING INVESTIGATED AS 'A SUSPECTED OVERDOSE': POLICE
Presley Gerber died one day after entering a treatment facility in Los Angeles, Calif. (Getty Images)
"I just don't assume what the cause of death is or that the facility failed them or the family ... don't think the family wasn't doing everything they had to do," Perlstein told Fox News Digital.
"It seems like, you know, in these situations the families do so much for the sick person, the person who was addicted."
He added, "By all accounts, they were a very loving, good family, and it's just real sad circumstance. It certainly caught a lot of people's attention. I'll tell you that much."
Gerber, the only son of supermodel Cindy Crawford and businessman Rande Gerber, died while staying at the rehabilitation facility, according to records from the Los Angeles County Medical Examiner.
KID ROCK CALLS PRESLEY GERBER’S DEATH A ‘TRAGEDY’ AS EX-GIRLFRIEND SAYS HE ‘DESERVED MORE TIME’

The treatment center's website says it draws "on our years of experience in addiction and mental health support," with "experienced staff has supported people with a wide variety of needs, from substance abuse and mental health, to trauma and eating disorders."
Cindy Crawford and husband Rande Gerber were seen at their late son Presley Gerber's home in Hollywood following his death at age 27. (RMBI/JOGA/JAPZ/Backgrid)
Gerber reportedly checked into the facility on Saturday night and died Sunday morning. Representatives for Resolutions Living did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Nicholas Kardaris, Ph.D., CEO and chief clinical officer of the New York Center for Living in Manhattan and a clinical professor at Stony Brook Medicine’s School of Social Welfare, cautioned against drawing conclusions from the fact that he died at a rehabilitation facility.
CINDY CRAWFORD’S SON PRESLEY GERBER SAID HE WAS ‘TERRIFIED’ IN RAW ADDICTION POST MONTHS BEFORE DEATH AT 27

As Gerber’s official cause of death has not yet been released, Kardaris — who has not treated Presley Gerber and is not connected to the case — noted that possible explanations could include an acute medical or cardiac event, an undiagnosed condition or a medication-related complication.
Presley Gerber was the only son of Cindy Crawford and Rande Gerber. (Gilbert Flores/WWD via Getty Images)
Presley Gerber died Sunday of a suspected drug overdose, according to police. He was 27. (Paul Archuleta)
People in residential treatment facilities may have complex medical histories, and some conditions may not be immediately apparent when someone enters a program.
"Younger people can sometimes die suddenly, and we don’t know whether they had an underlying medical issue," Kardaris said.
"It’s not impossible to have a medication-related event, particularly if someone has an underlying heart disorder," he continued. "Certain medications can trigger a cardiac episode."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
He added, "People are in rehab because they’re struggling with addiction. It doesn’t mean they’re cured of their addiction."

Another potential risk during rehab is withdrawal itself, which can range from uncomfortable to life-threatening depending on the substance involved and the person’s level of physical dependence, according to Kardaris.
Presley Gerber's death investigation is ongoing with limited information available, according to the medical examiner. (Jeff Spicer/Getty Images for Tommy Hilfiger)
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE
"People can die from withdrawal, but the substances that are most dangerous to withdraw [from] without proper medical supervision are benzodiazepines, such as Valium or Xanax, and alcohol," he said.
The deputy medical examiner (DME) told Fox News Digital that "the investigation is still ongoing and there is limited information available," and his cause of death has not yet been released.
The DME is in "the early stages of investigating the death of 27-year-old model Presley Gerber and limited information is currently available," according to a statement from the department.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"A deputy medical examiner performed an examination today and the cause and manner of death have been deferred, which means additional testing and/or studies were requested in order to make a determination."
Presley Gerber had been candid about past addiction issues. (Victor Boyko/Getty Images for Balmain)
They added, "Due to the ongoing death investigation, the DME cannot disclose what testing and/or studies were requested. Deferred cases can take a few months before a cause of death is determined."
Santa Monica Police Department officials are investigating the death as "a suspected overdose," according to a release from the department.
Officers responded to a report of a possible overdose at approximately 9:35 a.m., Sunday, Sept. 20. Upon arrival, officers located an adult male who was deceased.
At this time, there is no indication of foul play, and Gerber's case remains open. The facility has not been accused of wrongdoing.

A representative for the family told Fox News Digital, "The family is asking for privacy during this very difficult and painful time."
Fox News Digital's Melissa Rudy contributed to this report.

title: Ella Langley says 'Choosin' Texas' success is 'changing my life' after her song breaks Mariah Carey's record
summary: Ella Langley celebrated a career-defining milestone after “Choosin’ Texas" spent its 23rd week at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100.
story: Ella Langley speaks about her deep appreciation for supporters and how their connection transformed her path, while attending the 2026 iHeartRadio Music Awards.
Ella Langley knew "Choosin' Texas" was special. Even she couldn't have predicted just how far it would go.

On Tuesday night, Langley took to Instagram to celebrate making Billboard Hot 100 history this week when "Choosin' Texas" logged its 23rd week at No. 1, surpassing Mariah Carey's "All I Want for Christmas Is You" for the longest reign at the top of the chart.

"I'm genuinely trying to find the words to explain what's going on in my brain today," Langley began her video. "What? I don't know. Thank you so much. Thank you for loving this song, for listening to it. I feel like… I just don't even know what to say at this point. I'm running out of hyperboles to describe how I feel, so I will just let my dog in the background show you his excitement," she continued as her dog barked.
Ella Langley topped the Billboard Hot 100 charts for the 14th week in a row with her "Choosin' Texas" anthem. (John Schearer)

"Just thank you. Thank you so much. It's changing my life. It's changing the lives of the writers of this song. It's changing the lives of my family, and it is truly growing an atmosphere for something I'm gonna be able to do the rest of my life and I just… today doesn't feel like a real thing," Langley said. "It feels fake and somebody's going to come in and be like 'haha we're kidding the whole time just kidding.'"
ELLA LANGLEY SEEMINGLY FIRES BACK AFTER DOJA CAT'S BRUTAL TAKE ON HER CHART-TOPPING HIT
"I'm really excited to just experience a moment like this in my life," she said.
The country music star told her fans that she was going to celebrate tonight before ending with, "Choosin' T… that's the one huh?"
In a resurfaced interview with Billboard from March, when the song was still climbing, Langley admitted its success had already surpassed anything she imagined when she wrote it.
"When we wrote it, I knew it was going on the record. I honestly knew it was going to be the lead single," Langley told Billboard.

"And we love that song, but I don't think I could have ever imagined what's happening with it right now," she continued. "Like I said, every day I wake up, and it's doing something that I didn't even know was a goal that I could have had."
"It's just nuts," Langley added. "It's crazy to see the ownership that the fans have taken over it. And the different demographics of people listening to the song is so cool."
What seemed unimaginable to Langley in March has since become historic.
ELLA LANGLEY'S 'CHOOSIN' TEXAS' SPENDS 15 WEEKS AT NUMBER ONE ON THE BILLBOARD HOT 100
"Choosin' Texas" first entered the Hot 100 in November 2025, became Langley's first top 10 in January and reached No. 1 for the first time in February.
The song has also spent 41 weeks at No. 1 on Billboard's Hot Country Songs chart.
Long before it became a record breaker, however, "Choosin' Texas" began with a story about a kangaroo.
Langley recalled writing the song during her first songwriting retreat with country superstar Miranda Lambert and two other writers.

"So, I was on a writer's retreat with Miranda," Langley explained in the resurfaced Billboard interview. "This is our first time that we had written together, and obviously we were there with two others."

Ella Langley performs onstage during the 59th Annual Country Music Association Awards at Bridgestone Arena in Nashville, Tenn., on Nov. 19, 2025. (Kevin Mazur/Getty Images)
Billboard credits Langley, Lambert, Luke Dick and Joybeth Taylor as the four co-writers of "Choosin' Texas."
Langley said Lambert began telling her a story about a pet kangaroo.
"I learned at a young age she had a pet kangaroo and I wanted to ask her about it," Langley recalled. "So, I was like, 'Tell me about this kangaroo that you had. I need to know.'"
ELLA LANGLEY'S TEXAS PHOTO DUMP SENDS COUNTRY MUSIC FANS INTO A FRENZY ONLINE ON INSTAGRAM
Lambert told the group about once being pulled over with the kangaroo riding in the passenger seat and a dog in the back.

"She said she got pulled over and the kangaroo ended up getting her out of a ticket, but she's like, 'Of course, I had Texas plates on, too,'" Langley recalled.
ELLA LANGLEY JOINS MUSIC ROYALTY WITH 'INSANE' MILESTONE FOR 'CHOOSIN' TEXAS'
Ella Langley performs onstage at the Billboard Women in Music 2026 held at the Hollywood Palladium on April 29, 2026, in Los Angeles, Calif. (Rich Polk/Billboard via Getty Images)
That was enough to spark the song.
"And I went, 'Well, she's from Texas, I can tell,'" Langley said. "And just from that phrase, it kind of all hit us."
According to Langley, the melody came almost immediately, with Lambert helping develop the story behind it.
"And 45 minutes later, we had that song written," Langley said. "And it was just, it was such a cool experience."
Lambert's involvement didn't end in the writing room.
Langley told Billboard that the country superstar was executive producing her next record and had become someone she could turn to for advice.

"There's not a rulebook to this job," Langley said. "So to be able to have someone like her to ask questions and think, you know, is it, should I be doing this? She's like, 'Hell yeah, you should be doing this.'"

Miranda Lambert and Ella Langley pose in the winner's walk during the 61st Academy of Country Music Awards. (Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for ACM)
Even Lambert was surprised by what was happening with "Choosin' Texas."
"My team's calling me every day freaking out about this song," Langley recalled Lambert telling her.
At the time of the March interview, the song had reached No. 5 on the Hot 100.
"How crazy is that?" Langley said.
"And for me, like, what, me? You mean me?"
Six months later, "Choosin' Texas" stands alone as the longest-running No. 1 song in Hot 100 history.
Langley's historic week comes as she continues performing across the country.

title: Never smoked a cigarette? You could still be at higher risk for lung cancer
summary: Never-smokers carrying the rare EGFR T790M gene variant face 62 times the odds of lung cancer, a major study of 3.3 million people suggests.
story: Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel discusses a new study revealing a historic decline in adult cigarette smoking rates in the U.S. to under 10%.
A rare genetic mutation could put people at a dramatically higher risk of developing lung cancer even if they’ve never smoked.

A rare mutation in the gene EGFR T790M was found to increase lung cancer risk by 25 times compared with people who did not have the mutation, according to a new study published in the journal Science.
Among people who had never smoked, carriers of the mutation had about 62 times the odds of lung cancer compared with never-smokers who did not have it.
PANCREATIC CANCER VACCINE SHOWS PROMISE IN FIRST HUMAN TRIAL, PREVENTING DISEASE IN HIGH-RISK PATIENTS
The study, led by investigators at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and 23andMe Research Institute, analyzed data from more than 3.3 million people.
The gene variant showed no increased risk across 17 other cancers studied.
A rare genetic mutation could put people at a dramatically higher risk of developing lung cancer even if they’ve never smoked. (iStock)

"Today, lung cancer screening is driven almost entirely by smoking history," study co-author Jaclyn LoPiccolo, attending physician and lung cancer researcher at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, said in a press release.
CANCER WARNING SIGNS MAY APPEAR IN DNA YEARS BEFORE BLOOD TESTS DETECT TROUBLE

"Our findings raise the possibility that, in the future, screening could also be dictated by inherited genetic risk. If further studies confirm the benefit, people with EGFR T790M could be identified through genetic testing and offered personalized CT screening to identify lung cancers when they are at their most curable stage."
Among people who had never smoked, carriers of the mutation had about 62 times the odds of lung cancer compared with never-smokers who did not have it. (iStock)
Most U.S. carriers of the mutation were traced to a shared ancestry linked to British and Irish settlers in Southern Appalachia about 200–225 years ago, the researchers found.

The mutation remains rare nationwide, affecting roughly one in 15,000–16,000 people. It is more common in some parts of Southern Appalachia, where researchers estimate as many as one in 2,000 people may carry it.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"We found that the vast majority of carriers inherited the mutation from the same ancestral lineage," said LoPiccolo. "We could trace that lineage to British and Irish settlers in the United States and show that the mutation became enriched after a founder event and genetic bottleneck in Southern Appalachia about 200 years ago.
"It's a fascinating example of how human migration and genealogy can shape disease risk, generations later."
While the study establishes a strong association with lung cancer risk, it does not demonstrate that genetic testing improves mortality or other health outcomes. (iStock)
One of the "remarkable" findings of the study was the fact that a single mutation could have such a strong effect, according to Alexander Gusev, a quantitative geneticist at Dana-Farber.
"To my knowledge, it's one of the strongest, if not the strongest, cancer risk-increasing mutations that has ever been found," he said in the release.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"Smoking is bad for lung cancer. This mutation is bad for lung cancer. When you do both, your risk is the sum of those two risks," he added. "So, you definitely don't want to smoke."

The researchers suggest that people with a strong family history of lung cancer, multiple lung nodules or tumors or family roots in parts of the southeastern U.S. should consider speaking with a genetic counselor about whether genetic testing or lung cancer screening makes sense for them.
"It's a fascinating example of how human migration and genealogy can shape disease risk generations later."
There were some limitations to the study.
Because the mutation is so rare, researchers identified relatively few carriers even among the millions of participants, meaning the exact size of the increased risk remains uncertain.

The analysis also relied heavily on 23andMe research participants, who may not represent the broader population.
Because the mutation is much more common in certain parts of the U.S., the risk estimates may not apply equally to everyone, the researchers noted.

While the study establishes a strong association with lung cancer risk, it does not demonstrate that genetic testing improves mortality or other health outcomes.

title: Popular weight-loss drugs may play surprising role in cancer outcomes
summary: GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy may lower cancer risk by altering the body's immune response, but researchers say key clinical trials are needed.
story: Sai Yendamuri, M.D., a thoracic surgeon at Roswell Park Comprehensive Cancer Center in Buffalo, New York, speaks to Fox News Digital about whether weight-loss drugs could reduce cancer risk.
As GLP-1 medications continue reshaping the treatment of obesity and diabetes, researchers are also investigating whether the drugs could influence cancer risk and outcomes.
The American Association for Cancer Research's 2026 Cancer Progress Report, released earlier this month, noted that obesity is a major risk factor for many cancers.

As glucagon-like peptide-1 medications – including semaglutides like Ozempic and Wegovy, and tirzepatides like Mounjaro and Zepbound – are known to cause substantial weight loss and improve metabolic health, they have attracted significant interest among cancer researchers.
POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS MAY HELP PROTECT AGAINST A DEADLY DISEASE, DOCTOR SAYS
While the AACR report cited studies suggesting GLP-1 medications may reduce the risk of certain cancers, it emphasized that the overall evidence is mixed and more research is needed.
"Randomized clinical trials remain the gold standard ... however, such trials have not yet been conducted specifically to assess cancer outcomes associated with GLP-1 RA use," the report stated.
As GLP-1 medications continue reshaping the treatment of obesity and diabetes, researchers are also investigating whether the drugs could influence cancer risk and outcomes. (iStock)

Sai Yendamuri, M.D., a thoracic surgeon at Roswell Park Comprehensive Cancer Center in Buffalo, New York, reiterated that obesity is a leading cause of cancer, second to smoking. Additional risk factors include alcohol and poor nutrition, he noted, "which are all layered into obesity."

"So if obesity is related to cancer – both in terms of causing it and increasing its progression – the logical question is, would a drug that decreases obesity have an impact?" the doctor, who was not associated with the AACR report, said in an interview with Fox News Digital.
OZEMPIC-STYLE DRUGS LINKED TO MAJOR SLOWDOWN IN CANCER SPREAD, NEW STUDY FINDS
There are "many lines of evidence" that suggest this would be the case, Yendamuri suggested.
"For example, when people studied patients who were having metabolic surgery to decrease obesity, for example, the incidence of cancer decreased in those patients."
While the AACR report cited studies suggesting GLP-1 medications may reduce the risk of certain cancers, it emphasized that the overall evidence is mixed and more research is needed. (iStock)
Researchers then started looking at patients who were on GLP-1 receptor agonists, such as Ozempic.

"And then they compared the incidence of cancer in those patients to patients who were not taking GLP-1 receptor agonists – and many of those studies found that the risk of cancer was lower and the survival was higher in the patients taking GLP-1s," the doctor said.
DR OZ LINKS OBESITY TO CHRONIC DISEASE SURGE, SAYS GLP-1S CAN 'JUMPSTART' BETTER HEALTH

Although the majority of studies showed this effect, Yendamuri noted that some did not identify a relationship – and a couple of studies even showed an increased risk of some specific cancers, such as thyroid cancer.

"The reason you find this disconnect … is because these are retrospective studies," he said. "That is, they look at existing data, and they're trying to derive associations from existing data … but there are many other variables that can impact the result."
The American Association for Cancer Research's 2026 Cancer Progress Report, released earlier this month, noted that obesity is a major risk factor for many cancers. (iStock)
Yendamuri and his team of researchers have conducted their own studies of the relationship between obesity and lung cancer.
"We have found in every investigation we've done that obesity does increase the risk of lung cancer," he shared.
CANCER TREATMENT DELAYS SURGE ACROSS US AS DOCTOR WARNS SYSTEM ‘NEEDS FIXING IMMEDIATELY’

Obesity also depends on how it's defined and measured, Yendamuri noted. While body mass index (BMI) has traditionally been the standard measure, many obesity researchers are moving away from relying on BMI alone and instead using more precise assessments of body fat composition.
Yendamuri shared two key findings from his research.
"If someone's having a resection, a lung cancer surgery, for patients who are on GLP-1 receptor agonists, the recurrence rate seems to be lower."
"What we think is happening is that it changes the body’s immune response to cancer cells, and thereby improves its ability to fight cancer cells."
Additionally, patients with advanced-stage cancers who are in immunotherapy and taking GLP-1s had lower recurrence rates, he noted.
Based on preclinical laboratory studies, Yendamuri said he believes GLP-1 medications have only a limited direct effect on cancer cells.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"What we think is happening is that it changes the body’s immune response to cancer cells, and thereby improves its ability to fight cancer cells," he told Fox News Digital.
The effect may differ depending on the type of cancer, Yendamuri said, because the immune response is more important in some cancers than others.
The effect may differ depending on the type of cancer, an expert said, because the immune response is more important in some cancers than others. (iStock)
"For example, in some cancers like melanoma, we know that the immune response is incredibly important," he said.
Yendamuri acknowledged that at least some of the cancer benefit likely stems from weight loss.

"Not every patient who takes GLP-1 receptor agonists responds with a substantial weight loss, so in future trials, it would be interesting to see if the benefit for patients depends on the weight loss," he said.
"If those patients who have weight loss with GLP-1 receptor agonists have the same cancer benefit as patients who do not have weight loss, that will answer that question."

Depending on the outcomes of future trials, the doctor said he is hopeful that GLP-1 drugs could one day be regarded as a preventive mechanism for cancer.

"More and more, we are realizing that apart from the treatment that you get for cancer, lifestyle modifications – exercise, decreasing weight and now GLP-1 receptor agonists – will all have a role in both enhancing the treatment of cancer as well as preventing second cancers," he said.

title: Strokes nearly double among adults under a certain age in disturbing trend
summary: Stroke incidence among young adults more than doubled over three decades, with ischemic stroke and marijuana use surging, a new study reveals.
story: Dr. Jason A. Gluck, vice chair of the Heart & Vascular Institute and system chief of cardiology at AtlantiCare in New Jersey, discusses a recent study that found stroke incidence has more than doubled among young adults.
Stroke incidence more than doubled among young adults in a recent study.
Researchers at the University of Cincinnati analyzed data from 2,076 first-ever strokes among adults ages 20–54 in the Greater Cincinnati/Northern Kentucky region from 1993-1994 to 2020.
Over those three decades, the incidence increased from about 34 to 62 strokes per 100,000 people per year.
HEART ATTACKS AND STROKES RISING WITH EXTREME WEATHER EVENTS, RESEARCH SUGGESTS
The increase was primarily driven by ischemic stroke, which occurs when a blood vessel supplying the brain becomes blocked.
Among the younger adults who experienced strokes, there was an increase in hypertension, diabetes, atrial fibrillation (irregular heartbeat) and substance use.
Stroke incidence more than doubled among young adults in a recent study. (iStock)

"This has major implications, since young people who develop disability from a stroke may no longer be able to work or provide for their families," study co-author David J. Robinson, M.D., an assistant professor of clinical neurology and rehabilitation medicine at the University of Cincinnati College of Medicine, told Fox News Digital.
"We don't know for sure why strokes are becoming more common, and we really need to study this in more depth if we are going to reverse this trend."
8 COMMON FOOD PRESERVATIVES LINKED TO HIGHER RISK OF HIGH BLOOD PRESSURE AND HEART DISEASE
There was also a sharp increase in documented substance use, which rose from 4.6% to 40.2% in the study period, primarily marijuana.

"It's hard to say whether this is responsible for any of the rise in stroke; there is a relationship between marijuana use and stroke, but most of the evidence is with heavier use," Robinson said. "The relationship between marijuana use and cardiovascular disease needs more study so that we can properly advise our patients."
The increase was primarily driven by ischemic stroke, which occurs when a blood vessel supplying the brain becomes blocked. (iStock)
In contrast to younger adults, stroke rates declined among older adults, falling from about 619 to 453 strokes per 100,000 people per year.

Short-term survival after stroke also improved, the researchers found. The share of younger adults who died within 30 days of a stroke declined from 11.7% to 9.4% – primarily for bleeding-related strokes, including intracerebral and subarachnoid hemorrhages.
WHAT TO DO IF SOMEONE IS HAVING A STROKE, AFTER JILL BIDEN REVEALED DEBATE-NIGHT FEARS

"Our study might provide evidence that we have gotten better at treating people who have hemorrhagic strokes and helping them survive, which is encouraging," said Robinson. "Still, prevention is the most important thing to focus on, because just surviving a stroke doesn't mean you aren't left without disability."
The findings were published in the journal Neurology on Sept. 23.
‘Uncommon, not zero risk’

Dr. Jason A. Gluck, vice chair of the Heart & Vascular Institute and system chief of cardiology at AtlantiCare in New Jersey, noted that while stroke is still uncommon in young adults, that doesn’t mean they have zero risk.

"The concerning findings in this particular trial is that stroke rates are moving in the wrong direction for the younger population," Gluck, who was not involved in the research, told Fox News Digital.
The share of younger adults who died within 30 days of a stroke declined from 11.7% to 9.4% – primarily for bleeding-related strokes, including intracerebral and subarachnoid hemorrhages. (iStock)
"While many of the risk factors are things that we can identify and treat before a stroke occurs, when you're young, sometimes you don't know about it – so awareness is key."
Risk factors are pervasive across all age groups, the doctor noted.
POPULAR ARTIFICIAL SWEETENER LINKED TO POTENTIALLY DANGEROUS HEART RISK

"The same things that happen to 70-year-olds can happen at 40 – if you have high blood pressure, if you have diabetes, if you’re smoking, if there's obesity, abnormal cholesterol and activity, all those things can lead to [stroke]," he warned.
"Vascular disease doesn't suddenly begin when you're 65; it develops over time."
Study limitations
The main limitation of the study is that it did not include comparable risk factors for people without stroke.

"We can't say for sure how many of the stroke risk factors are changing in people without stroke in our region," Robinson noted. "This makes it really hard to determine what is causing this rising incidence. We will need to look in other studies to really understand the ‘why’ of this trend."
"Vascular disease doesn't suddenly begin when you're 65; it develops over time," one expert said. (iStock)

Also, the findings may have been affected by changes in medical documentation and diagnostic methods over the nearly three decades. One example provided was an increase in MRI use, which could potentially improve the detection of stroke. It was also possible that the rise in substance use was due to increased documentation or disclosure.
The study was also geographically limited, including just five counties in one U.S. state.
"While stroke is still relatively uncommon in younger individuals, it can happen and be really devastating," Robinson said.

The doctor emphasized that hypertension is the risk factor most tightly associated with stroke.
"Younger people may not have a lot of opportunities to get their blood pressure and other risk factors screened, and we need to come up with solutions that can meet them where they are," he said.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Robinson recommended using the American Heart Association’s "Life’s Essential 8," which is a checklist for optimizing your cardiovascular health.

"It includes blood pressure control along with eating better, being less sedentary, quitting any tobacco products, sleeping well, managing your weight, controlling cholesterol and managing blood sugar."
The increase was primarily driven by ischemic stroke, which occurs when a blood vessel supplying the brain becomes blocked. (iStock)
Gluck recommends using the "BE FAST" guide to determine whether someone may be having a stroke, as follows.
B: Balance suddenly offE: Eyes or vision change, where you suddenly can't see the way normally canF: Facial droopingA: Arm weaknessS: Speech difficultyT: Time to call 911

T: Time to call 911

"If you're having these symptoms or your loved one is having these symptoms, don't drive yourself to the hospital," he advised. "Call 911. Be fast."
