title: Ole Miss names students found dead as official addresses potential for foul play
summary: It remains unclear whether the deaths of Ole Miss students are connected, according to Lafayette County authorities.
story: Editor-in-Chief Regan Settle of Ole Miss's student-run news organization The Daily Mississippian, highlights growing student frustration after two campus drug overdose deaths, pressing university leaders to communicate directly.

OXFORD, Miss. — The two University of Mississippi students found dead under suspicious circumstances in recent days have been identified by the school — which also said the names were being released with their families' approval.
Robert Strang, a 20-year-old from Atlanta, is the older of the two victims. The second student was as Aidan Hamilton, an 18-year-old freshman from Colorado.

"We are heartbroken by the loss of our dear son and are trying to process this unimaginable loss," Strang's family spokesman Scott Sayres told Fox News Digital Thursday. "We are deeply grateful for the incredible outpouring of love, prayers and support by so many beloved friends and family. Their kindness has meant more to our family than we can ever express."

Hamilton's family said in a statement that "Aidan was a bright, wonderful young man who was taken too soon. He is greatly missed. We thank everyone for their prayers and support and ask that you respect our family’s privacy during this time of great loss."
Both families have asked for privacy and compassion as they mourn the losses of their sons.
TWO OLE MISS STUDENTS FOUND DEAD AS PACKAGED KRATOM IS RECOVERED AT TWO SITES: OFFICIALS
Robert Strang pictured in an undated family photo. The 20-year-old University of Mississippi junior died under suspicious circumstances. (Strang family)

Separately, Commissioner of the Mississippi Department of Public Safety Sean Tindell told Fox News Digital that while authorities haven't uncovered any indications of foul play, they haven't ruled it out either.
"Until the autopsy is reported, and the investigators have an opportunity to get statements and collect evidence, then that final determination will not be made until later," he said.

Without the toxicology reports, it's also too early to determine whether kratom or other drugs were involved in the deaths. Police previously said that they found packages of kratom, which is commercially available in many places but not Lafayette County, at both scenes.

Aidan Hamilton, an 18-year-old University of Mississippi freshman, appears in these images that his mother posted to Facebook. He is one of two Ole Miss students who died under suspicious circumstances this week. (Facebook/ Kathie Mac Donald Hamilton)

He also said that both deaths happened at around the same time, or at least within a few hours, which was also suspicious. However, he said he expects the autopsy reports to give investigators a more specific window.

"The timing of it is suspicious, but I don't know that they have any direct relation other than if they both had ingested the substance from the same source," he said. "Then at some point we would try to track it back to that source and take appropriate action."

Stewart Hall, a dorm building on the University of Mississippi campus where an 18-year-old student is believed to have died on Monday. Dispatch records show first responders arrived within a minute of being sent to the address. (Adam Sabes/Fox News Digital)
Social media posts from the Ole Miss chapter of the Phi Delta Theta fraternity identify Strang as one of seven co-chairmen of the 2026 Rush, when new members are recruited.

"As our university community continues to mourn the recent tragic loss of two of our students, I encourage everyone to remember that at the center of this are two grieving families, who are processing the unimaginable loss of a child," the school's Vice Chancellor for Student Affairs Dr. Shawnboda Mead said in a statement Thursday afternoon.

"We have been in touch with the families to offer our deepest sympathies and share university support and resources. Until now, we have upheld their wishes not to release the names of their students," she continued. "Today, the families of Aidan Hamilton, a freshman from Englewood, Colo., and Robert Strang, a junior from Atlanta, have given us permission to share their names. The families have asked for privacy as they grieve."
Mead continued to urge the public not to rely on speculation or unverified information about the case as law enforcement continues to investigate both deaths.

"We offer heartfelt condolences to the families, friends and classmates of Aidan and Robert," she said. "While there are no words that can alleviate the tremendous sorrow they are experiencing, please keep them close in your thoughts and prayers during this time of immense grief."
Phi Delta Theta's Ole Miss chapter also put out a statement after the university, asking for prayers for both victims.

"Phi Delta Theta joins the University of Mississippi and the broader Ole Miss community in mourning Robert and Aidan Hamilton and extending our deepest sympathies to their families, friends, chapter brothers, classmates, and all those who knew and loved them."
General view of Stewart Hall, Oxford, MS, September 24, 2026.  (Rashid Umar Abbasi for Fox News)
Strang was discovered at an off-campus home, according to the Lafayette County Coroner's Office. Hamilton, 18, is believed to have been found at Stewart Hall, a male dorm on the Ole Miss campus.
OLE MISS DEATHS, DRUGGINGS HAVE 'EPOPLE SCARED TO LEAVE' DORMS AS BARS, GREEK LIFE CLAMP DOWN

The Lafayette County Coroner's Office previously told Fox News that an 18-year-old had been found in a dorm room and the 20-year-old victim was recovered at an off-campus home. Both deaths are being investigated by the county's narcotics task force, and it's unclear whether they were connected.
SEND US A TIP

Authorities found packages of kratom, a commercially available drug that has been derided as "gas station heroin," at both scenes, however its role in either death was not immediately clear. Campus Greek life leaders have previously circulated a warning about a synthetic opioid called cychlorphine.
MANHATTAN PROSTITUTE PLEADS GUILTY TO KILLING 3 MEN WITH FENTANYL-LACED DRUGS IN ROBBERY SCHEME
Cychlorphine can be treated with Narcan but sometimes requires multiple doses, students were told. It also may not show up on common drug-detecting strips used to find fentanyl contamination.
Mississippi Gov. Tate Reeves gestures and speaks during the Neshoba County Fair in Philadelphia, Miss., on Thursday, June 25, 2026. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST
Students are being urged to avoid all drugs.
CHINESE NATIONALS ACCUSED OF SMUGGLING SYNTHETIC DRUGS INTO US PRISONS ON DRUG-SOAKED PAPER

Gov. Tate Reeves said Wednesday that state investigators were assisting local authorities, and that they would try and expedite the toxicology reports on both victims. Such reports typically take weeks to complete.

No official cause and manner of death have been given for either victim as of Thursday morning.

title: Texas triple murderer uses last words before execution to send message to death row inmates
summary: Ker'Sean Ramey received lethal injection at Huntsville prison, one week after accomplice LeJames Norman was executed for the same triple killing.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A man convicted of murdering three people in their apartment while searching for drugs to steal was executed in Texas on Wednesday evening, a week after his accomplice was put to death for the same killings.
Ker'Sean Ramey, 41, died by lethal injection at the state penitentiary in Huntsville and was pronounced dead at 6:34 p.m. CDT, The Associated Press reported.
In the execution chamber, a prison chaplain rested his hand on Ramey's shoulder before leading him in a brief prayer. The warden then asked Ramey if he had any last words, the AP reported.
Ramey praised God and thanked his friends, family and fellow death row inmates, whom he called his brothers.
This photo provided by the Texas Department of Criminal Justice shows Ker'Sean Ramey on Oct. 31, 2022. (Texas Department of Criminal Justice via AP)
ARIZONA EXECUTES MAN WHO KILLED VICTIM BY DOUSING HIM IN GASOLINE AND SETTING HIM ON FIRE IN 2002 ATTACK

"To the brothers on Texas death row that grew up with me, that poured into me and showed what it means to be a man, because I came in young, and didn’t understand what manhood was... to you brothers... I greatly appreciate you," Ramey said moments before the injection was prepared.
As the pentobarbital took effect, Ramey took a deep breath, sputtered and began snoring. After 10 loud snores and two that were barely audible, he went still.
He was pronounced dead 14 minutes after the injection was first administered.
Ramey became the sixth inmate executed in Texas this year, with the state set to carry out three more lethal injections over the next two months.

In January 2007, Ramey was convicted and sentenced to death for the August 2005 shootings of Samuel Roberts, 24, Tiffani Peacock, 18, and Celso Lopez, 38, at a home they shared in Edna, a small rural city about 100 miles southwest of Houston.
The state of Texas execution chamber in Huntsville, Texas, is seen on May 27, 2008. (AP Photo/Pat Sullivan)
74-YEAR-OLD BECOMES FLORIDA'S OLDEST INMATE EXECUTED AFTER 1982 KILLING OF TEEN
LeJames Norman, Ramey's accomplice, lived across the street from the house and the two came to believe there was cocaine there, according to court records.
On Aug. 24, 2005, the men walked over to the home while wearing masks and knocked on the door. After Lopez answered the door, they forced their way inside, records show.

After finding no drugs, the two men fatally shot Lopez, then killed Peacock and Roberts when they arrived at the home. Before fleeing for good, Ramey returned and shot the victims again to ensure they were dead, according to court documents.
Norman was executed on Sept. 16 at the Huntsville prison, where all executions are carried out in Texas.
The Huntsville Unit prison is seen in Huntsville, Texas, on Sept. 14, 2024. (Francois Picard/AFP)
MANHATTAN PROSTITUTE PLEADS GUILTY TO KILLING 3 MEN WITH FENTANYL-LACED DRUGS IN ROBBERY SCHEME

Hours before Ramey was put to death, the Supreme Court rejected his final appeal. Ramey's attorneys argued jurors never heard mitigating evidence about his upbringing, including that he endured physical abuse as a child and grew up in poverty.
State prosecutors urged the Supreme Court to reject the appeal, calling it "meritless" and arguing the record showed Ramey had exhibited an escalating pattern of criminal behavior.

Norman was arrested about five months after the killings while attempting to re-enter the United States from Mexico, where he had fled. During Ramey's January 2007 trial, Norman testified that both men took part in the shootings, while Ramey's attorneys argued Norman was solely responsible.
This photo provided by the Texas Department of Criminal Justice shows LeJames Norman on Feb. 28, 2024. (Texas Department of Criminal Justice via AP)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Ramey's former girlfriend testified that she was with him when he threw two handguns into a lake after the killings and that he later gave her a detailed account of his role in the crime.
Norman pleaded guilty to capital murder and was sentenced to death in December 2008.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Mistress says she gave ‘American Idol’ contestant ultimatum before wife’s killing blew up affair
summary: Caleb Flynn's mistress testified he talked about wanting Ashley Flynn dead and once said he was thinking about ways to kill her before the shooting.
story: Alleigha Botner, ex-mistress of former 'American Idol' contestant Caleb Flynn, delivers emotional testimony during his murder trial. Fox News' Garrett Tenney reports the latest and Fox News contributor Paul Mauro provides his analysis.

Former "American Idol" contestant Caleb Flynn told his mistress he stayed up until 4 a.m. "literally thinking of ways to kill" his wife and "not go to jail," one of a series of messages read to jurors Thursday in his Ohio murder trial.
Alleigha Botner returned to the witness stand for a second day and walked jurors through months of messages in which Flynn allegedly talked repeatedly about wanting Ashley Flynn dead or gone.
In one May 2025 message, Flynn allegedly wrote, "If I could literally kill her and not go to hell, I would do it in a heartbeat."
TEACHER FOUND DEAD WITH THROAT SLIT; DETECTIVES SCRUTINIZE HUSBAND’S SHIFTING STORY
Days later, he allegedly wrote, "I hate her, loathe her. I want her dead."

Caleb Flynn becomes emotional in court during his murder trial in Ohio. Flynn is accused of killing his wife, Ashley Flynn, in February 2026 and staging the scene to look like a break-in. (COURTESY: WKEF)
The messages became even more explicit in June, when Flynn allegedly told Botner, "Please hire someone to take [her] out. I need you in my life, I need you."

OHIO MAN CONVICTED AFTER TRYING TO SHOOT EX-WIFE AT POINT-BLANK RANGE INSIDE RESTAURANT IN CHILLING VIDEO

Jurors also heard that Flynn and Botner routinely deleted messages throughout their relationship.

Asked when she advised Flynn how to delete data from his devices, Botner responded, "Multiple times."

Botner also testified that on the night before Ashley's killing, she used ChatGPT to research whether messages documenting the affair could be permanently deleted and sent Flynn screenshots of the results.

The two exchanged roughly 107,000 messages while routinely deleting their conversations.

That day, she testified, Flynn told her he was "filing [for divorce] from Ashley" and was "actually leaving her this time."

But Ritter said Flynn's attorneys can argue prosecutors cherry-picked the most damaging language from more than 100,000 messages and that Flynn was talking about leaving Ashley, not killing her, when he discussed what would happen Feb. 16.

OXFORD, Miss. – An Ole Miss student says she was drugged at a bar over the weekend, days before two students were found dead, as bars around Oxford tighten security with fears running rampant through the college town.

Lafayette County Metro Narcotics said in a news release that investigators are looking into the deaths of two college-aged individuals whose bodies were discovered at separate locations. Authorities have not established a connection between the deaths, though packaged kratom purchased from a retail store was recovered in each investigation.
"We do not have confirmed information indicating that kratom or any other substance was a contributing factor in either death," the agency said.
WHAT IS KRATOM? RISKS OF POPULAR SUBSTANCE REVEALED AFTER COLLEGE STUDENTS' DEATHS
Fans enjoy tailgating before the Mississippi Rebels play the LSU Tigers at The Grove near Vaught-Hemingway Stadium in Oxford, Miss., on Sept. 30, 2023. (Getty Images)

"Later into that night, around the time when the game ended, I do not remember a single thing. And I was told by a boy that was there that I fell down," Harvey said.
TWO OLE MISS STUDENTS FOUND DEAD AS PACKAGED KRATOM IS RECOVERED AT TWO SITES: OFFICIALS
Ole Miss, also known as the University of Mississippi, expects an immense turnout of attendees for the TPUSA event featuring JD Vance and Erika Kirk. (Fox News Digital)

STUDENTS AT TOP PARTY COLLEGE ON EDGE AFTER RAPE, STRANGULATION REPORTED IN CAMPUS HOUSING

title: Florida couple recounts 'miraculous' rescue after surviving harrowing lightning strike during evening stroll
summary: Police bodycam video captured the frantic response after Aaron and Clare Walenga were struck on a popular trail in Winter Garden.
story: In an interview with Fox News Digital, Aaron and Clare Walenga said they were walking hand in hand in Winter Garden after dropping off their children at church when lightning struck them, leaving Clare unconscious and Aaron unable to move.

A Florida couple said they experienced nothing short of a miracle earlier this month when a bolt of lightning suddenly struck them during an evening stroll and sparked a frantic rescue by several good Samaritans whose heroism was caught on camera.

In an interview with Fox News Digital, Aaron Walenga, 48, and his wife, Clare, 43, recounted the harrowing moment in Winter Garden that left Aaron disoriented and paralyzed on the ground, police bodycam video shows, as bystanders rushed in to perform lifesaving measures on his unconscious wife.
"I couldn't move the way I wanted to," Aaron said. "I'm trying to get up. I am trying to get to Clare … I'm trying to talk, and I'm not really able to."
Aaron and Clare said the incident happened Sept. 2, after the couple dropped off their three children at a weekly church youth group gathering.
DASHCAM CAPTURES TERRIFYING MOMENT LIGHTNING NEARLY STRIKES UTAH TRUCK DRIVER

Aaron and Clare Walenga, center, reunite with the four good Samaritans who helped save their lives after the Florida couple was struck by lightning on Sept. 2. They were identified as Charlotte, Michael, Amber and Tiffany. (Walenga family)
"We dropped our kids off at church, and we use that as our date night, and we looked forward to it," he said. "So we went out and had dinner and then, we love to go for a walk."
As they walked hand in hand along the popular West Orange Trail, a nearby storm quickly rolled in and a bolt of lightning struck the couple without warning.
The next thing Aaron remembers was waking up in severe pain and confused.

"My first thought was that we got hit by a car," he said. "I thought maybe a car just ran us over from behind because getting struck by lightning is nothing that would even enter our minds," Aaron said.
MONTANA TEEN THROWS LASSO TO MAN IN YELLOWSTONE RIVER IN SPLIT-SECOND RESCUE
While still disoriented, Aaron said he saw bystanders and first responders tending to his unresponsive wife.

Four good Samaritans had apparently rushed to the scene, immediately calling 911 and performing CPR on Clare before responders arrived roughly 10 minutes later, the couple said. Witnesses told Clare that she had turned blue and stopped breathing for three to four minutes.

"I like to talk about the amount of bravery that they showed… they could see the fence beside them that lit up," Aaron said. "It was a big moment to turn around and then go, 'Hey, I think we need to go that direction.' And they did."

A hospital visit revealed that Aaron suffered fractured eye sockets, a broken nose, damaged teeth, facial cuts and burns on his hand and wrists, where he was holding an umbrella and wearing an Apple Watch.
Aaron and Clare Walenga recover in the hospital after the Florida couple was struck by lightning on Sept. 2. (Walenga family)

Despite undergoing a traumatic event, Aaron and Clare described their recovery as "miraculous," noting that they suffered serious conditions, including brain bleeds and heart damage, that they said completely healed within two days.
"We're just seeing miracle after miracle and just too many divine things in this unfortunate circumstance to not be noted," Clare said.

"We both had brain bleeds, and then I also suffered heart damage. And then when they followed up again two days later, it was healed. Neither of us had any brain bleed damage and my heart situation completely healed," she added.
Clare, who suffered intermittent memory loss, regained her full memory roughly two days later.
"God's not done with me yet," Clare said, adding that she feels immense gratitude to be alive.
DR. MARC SIEGEL: 'THE ANGELS AMONG US' -- A DYING WOMAN, THE SHOFAR AND THE MIRACLE THAT FOLLOWED
Aaron and Clare Walenga pose with their daughter and two sons at a home. (Walenga family)
Since the incident, the family said they have built a strong relationship with the good Samaritans who stepped in that day, adding that they are even planning to return to the trail in a few weeks.
The couple said they are overwhelmed by the support they have received from their local church, neighborhood and school communities.
Their pastor also helped bring their children safely home on the night of the lightning strike.
"Our neighbors are taking care of our yard and our pool for us, so it's just so many things happening without us even asking," Aaron said.
Aaron and Clare Walenga pose with their family in front of an Air Force jet. Aaron served in the Air Force for 24 years before retiring two years ago. (Walenga family)

"It's very humbling to know that people out there really care for you, and to see the church the way it's supposed to be, where it's not just in a building. It's really the people that are around you, and it's been amazing to watch."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Throughout the ordeal, the couple said they never felt hopeless, crediting their faith for helping them through the shocking experience.
"We've never asked ‘Why me?’" Aaron said. "We never got upset, we never felt hopeless. We really felt like even though it was a hard situation… God's been with us and there's a purpose behind it."
Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital

title: Parents accuse Oregon hospital of making them drive dead baby home to Seattle: lawsuit
summary: A Seattle couple's $10 million lawsuit alleges Salem Health staff pressured them to transport their deceased baby's body home in their personal vehicle.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A Seattle couple is suing after hospital staff in Oregon told them to drive the body of their nearly 9-month-old son four hours home in their private car following his sudden death in an emergency room.

Aleksandr and Nataliya Yeremeyev filed a $10 million lawsuit against Salem Health and Dr. Stefani Sorensen. The parents had allegedly sought respectful and dignified care and transportation of the remains of their son, Michael, but the lawsuit alleges staff insisted they bring the body back home with them.
Michael was born with Down syndrome and spent the first six months of his life at Seattle Children's Hospital.

"His parents had made sure that he had received really excellent care. So, I think it was a really, really sad and just very tragic way for his life to end and for it to be so undignified right there at the end," Anna Bruckenhoefer, the family's attorney, said in a statement, according to Fox 13.
TWO FAMILIES SUE NORTH DAKOTA HOSPITAL ON ALLEGATIONS BABIES WERE SWITCHED AT BIRTH

A Seattle couple is suing after hospital staff in Oregon told them to drive the body of their nearly 9-month-old son four hours home in their private car following his sudden death in an emergency room. (Google Maps)

On September 22, 2024, the family was visiting Salem, Oregon, for a religious retreat when Michael developed rapid, shallow breathing late at night and was rushed to the emergency room at Salem Health Hospital, where he died, according to the complaint.

When the parents asked how to arrange respectful transport to send Michael’s body back home to Seattle, hospital staff allegedly pushed back on the suggestion to contact a local funeral home because it would be "too expensive" and instead pressured the family to bring their son’s body with them in their own car, which they ended up doing due to feeling like they had no other option.

"They have repeatedly asked the hospital for assistance in helping them with what are the next steps," Bruckenhoefer said. "This was all occurring overnight. They felt rushed that they had to make quick decisions and the hospital left them with no choice other than to take Michael's body with them and head back to Seattle."
Aleksandr drove about four hours from Salem to Seattle with his son’s body laid across the backseat, while his wife and other children followed in a separate car.
FAMILY OF TODDLER FOUND ALIVE IN MORGUE AFTER BEING DECLARED DEAD PLANS LEGAL ACTION
Aleksandr and Nataliya Yeremeyev filed a $10 million lawsuit against Salem Health and Dr. Stefani Sorensen. (Google Maps)

He suffered severe emotional distress as he feared police stops, car crashes and the visible deterioration of his child's body, according to the lawsuit. When he arrived at a Seattle funeral home, the father had to clean bodily fluids that leaked onto the seat during the trip.

"It is legal in the state of Oregon and in the state of Washington to transport a deceased with the proper permits. But that is not what our clients wanted to do here. They were looking for help. They were looking for guidance. They were looking for the hospital to tell them, "These are the next steps,'" Bruckenhoefer said. "This is a hospital. It's an emergency department. Unfortunately, death is something that they are accustomed to and that they deal with. They should have had procedures and protocols in place to assist the Yeremeyev’s while they were dealing with literally the worst moment of their lives. Instead, what they did is they just compounded their grief by essentially telling them that they were on their own in this."
"No parents, no loved ones should ever be placed in the position that the Yeremeyev’s were placed in," Bruckenhoefer added. "Just completely surprised that something like this would happen in 2026."

The lawsuit names Salem Health Hospitals & Clinics, Salem Health, Salem Emergency Physicians Service and Sorensen as defendants, alleging direct negligence, vicarious liability, and a breach of the heightened duty of care owed to bereaved parents for the respectful treatment and custody of a child's body.
Aleksandr Yeremeyev drove about four hours from Salem to Seattle with his son’s body laid across the backseat. (Google Maps)
The family is seeking $10 million in non-economic damages for severe emotional distress and psychological trauma, although they plan to amend the complaint to include punitive damages.
Salem Health Hospital said out of respect for privacy and because the matter is in litigation, it is unable to discuss the details of the child's care.

"Salem Hospital responded in accordance with the family’s wishes and followed both hospital policy and Oregon state law in consultation with the appropriate local authorities, including the medical examiner," Salem Health told Fox 13 in a statement.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Care with respect is a guiding principle of clinical practice at Salem Hospital and remains central to how we support patients and families during some of life's most difficult moments. We recognize the profound grief families experience following the loss of a loved one and treat every patient and family with empathy, dignity, and respect," the statement continued.

title: Tennessee cops raided man's home after he criticized officer for speeding: lawsuit
summary: A First Amendment lawsuit alleges Kingsport Police in Tennessee raided Joshua Gibbons' home after he filmed and criticized a cop speeding at night.
story: Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression Senior Attorney Adam Steinbaugh said police are required by the First Amendment to tolerate both fair and unfair criticism.
A Tennessee man who was arrested in a pre-dawn raid after he filmed and criticized a police officer sued the police department alleging it violated his First Amendment right to free expression.

The civil lawsuit against the city of Kingsport, its police chief and its officers was filed by the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression (FIRE) in 2023 on behalf of Joshua Gibbons, but he is only now making the complaint public after he was successful in having his conviction overturned and the remaining charge dismissed by the Tennessee Court of Criminal Appeals.

"They tried to intimidate me, but I’m not backing down," Gibbons said in a statement. "I can’t let this injustice stand, because my family doesn’t feel safe anymore. There’s no coming back from that raid on our home. They sent eight heavily armed officers to arrest me because I embarrassed them."

In October 2022, Gibbons filmed a Kingsport Police Department SUV speeding at night without lights or sirens, which the lawsuit alleges violated department policy and state law. He followed the vehicle and approached the officer at a fast food drive-thru, where he filmed his brief criticism of the officer’s conduct.
POLICE FATALLY SHOOT SWORD WIELDING MAN AFTER WOMAN FOUND TRAPPED IN CAR, OFFICIALS SAY
Joshua Gibbons sued the police department over allegations it violated his First Amendment rights. (Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression)

"When he caught up with the officer, the officer did the right thing. He ignored Joshua Gibbons, didn't arrest him, didn't view it as a crime, and went and got his hamburger," FIRE senior attorney Adam Steinbaugh told Fox News Digital.
Gibbons, who uploads videos of police on duty as a way to hold them accountable, later published a second video of an officer giving him the middle finger.

A fellow citizen later complained to the department about the officer’s conduct, and the department responded by searching Gibbons’ YouTube channel for something to use against him, according to FIRE.
The department found the video of their own officer speeding. But instead of disciplining the officer, officers were sent to arrest Gibbons.

"The First Amendment protects the right not only to criticize and film police, but also to post it online. The police department didn't treat this as a crime until Joshua posted this online and embarrassed the department," Steinbaugh said.
Joshua Gibbons faced two trials over nearly four years before a Tennessee appellate court recently dismissed the charges. (Zelina Photography)
Steinbaugh also said the case was "as lawless as it was hypocritical" and that the department’s actions "were all to make an example out of a critic."

According to the lawsuit, within two hours of being "made aware" of Gibbons’ video of the speeding officer, an arrest warrant for Gibbons was obtained for speeding, using a cell phone while driving and disorderly conduct. The warrant was obtained from a court clerk rather than a judge, according to FIRE.

Just before dawn the following morning, eight armed officers were captured on security and cell phone footage raiding Gibbons’ house and arresting him in front of his elderly mother and his daughter, just nine days after he filmed and criticized the speeding officer.
Gibbons then faced two trials over nearly four years before a Tennessee appellate court recently dismissed the charges.

"That's a long process that can take a mental toll on someone. I think that Joshua wants to send a message to this department. I think he wants to see some reforms to this department, and we're happy to support him," Steinbaugh said.
TENNESSEE OFFICIAL SAYS FLOCK CEO SHOULD BE HANGED 'PUBLICLY FOR TREASON' AS CONTROVERSIAL CAMERAS FACE REVOLT
The civil lawsuit was filed against the city of Kingsport, its police chief and its officers. (Kingsport Police)

In the first trial, a judge acquitted him of the speeding and cell phone charges but found Gibbons guilty of disorderly conduct, saying he was "offended by the way" Gibbons was "talking to that officer." Gibbons appealed to the county circuit court, and a jury found him guilty of disorderly conduct.

But in June, the Court of Criminal Appeals of Tennessee unanimously overturned the verdict and dismissed the disorderly conduct charge, finding there was "no evidence" that Gibbons’ criticism of the officer "prevented any person from doing any lawful activity."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The court said Gibbons "did not threaten anyone, did not engage in any violent behavior, and did not create a physically offensive or hazardous condition." The court noted that even "'profane and insulting' words alone will not rise to the level of a crime, particularly when uttered against the police, who 'are trained to exercise a higher degree of restraint than the average citizen.'"

"If you are a law enforcement officer, you are required by your uniform and by the First Amendment to tolerate criticism. Some of that's going to be fair criticism, some of it's going to be unfair criticism. But you don't get to go and arrest people for it. That's the message we want to send to this department and to departments around the country," Steinbaugh said.
Kingsport Police did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment in time for publication.

title: ‘Wave of freedom’ sweeps Latin America as Trump ally takes fight to Marxist terror group
summary: José Manuel Restrepo says Colombian forces, not American troops, will lead operations against armed groups under Trump's Shield of the Americas.
story: Colombian Vice President José Manuel Restrepo told Fox News Digital his government supports President Donald Trump’s new regional security alliance, but said Colombian forces — not U.S. troops — will carry out operations inside the country.

UNITED NATIONS — Colombian Vice President José Manuel Restrepo said his country is embracing President Donald Trump’s push for a new security alliance across the Western Hemisphere, but drew a clear line on the role American forces would play inside Colombia, telling Fox News Digital that Colombian troops — not U.S. forces — will carry out operations against the country’s armed groups.

Restrepo spoke with Fox News Digital in an on-camera interview days after joining Trump and other regional leaders at a Shield of the Americas meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York, where Trump called the initiative the "largest and most powerful alliance for economic and national security ever to convene in the Western Hemisphere."
Trump urged members to treat what he called "narco terrorists" as common threats and impose sanctions on U.S.-designated terrorist organizations.

Restrepo said he personally discussed the region’s changing political and security landscape with Trump. The shift in Colombia comes amid a broader political realignment across Latin America, with De La Espriella’s June victory adding Colombia to a group of countries including Argentina, Chile, Ecuador, Bolivia and Panama that have moved to the right, fueled in part by voter concerns over crime, economic weakness and political instability.
TRUMP ALLY 'EL TIGRE' SWORN IN AS COLOMBIA'S NEW PRESIDENT AMID CONTINENT'S RIGHTWARD SHIFT

President Donald Trump, center, Dominican Republic President Luis Abinader, second from left, Argentina's President Javier Milei, El Salvador's President Nayib Bukele, Guyana's President Mohamed Irfaan Ali, Costa Rica's President Rodrigo Chaves Robles, Bolivia's President Rodrigo Paz and Chile's President-elect Jose Antonio Kast pose for a family photo during the Shield of the Americas" Summit in Doral, Fla., on Saturday, March 7, 2026. (Kevin Lamarque/Reuters)

"There is a wave of freedom, a wave of democracy, a wave of free market. … There is a new momentum for the region and we have to take advantage of that momentum. That's what I said to President Trump," Restrepo told Fox News Digital. "If we want to keep and preserve democracy in the region, the Shield of the Americas is going to be the best opportunity to do it."
Asked what Trump told him, Restrepo said the president agreed and expressed respect for Colombian President Abelardo De La Espriella.
"Colombia is a new partner. In my opinion, it's one of the most important partners for the United States in the region," Restrepo said.
That partnership is already being tested in the fight against drug trafficking and armed groups.
WHITE HOUSE HIGHLIGHTS 'STEEPEST' EVER DECLINE IN US CASUALTIES FROM CARTELS AMID BOAT STRIKES

A police officer stands guard on a street following a military operation against the drug-related armed group Conquering Self Defense Forces of the Sierra Nevada (ACSN) in Santa Marta, Colombia on September 23, 2026. Colombia's President Abelardo de la Espriella sent troops into Santa Marta after an armed group attacked shops and burnt vehicles across the Caribbean city, he announced on September 22, 2026. The chaos followed an earlier announcement by the president that authorities had killed 13 members of the self-styled Conquering Self Defense Forces of the Sierra Nevada (ACSN), an armed group which controls cocaine trafficking routes. (Marco Perdomo / AFP via Getty Images)

In August, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Colombia had authorized "joint military operations to destroy terrorists and terror networks" and told reporters that Washington had discussed possible joint strikes against groups including the National Liberation Army, or ELN, which the U.S. designates as a terrorist organization, and remnants of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia.

"Designated terrorist organizations, with partnered governments, will be legitimate targets of the United States government," including in Colombia, Hegseth said when asked whether such operations were expected, according to Reuters.
But when pressed by Fox News Digital on whether joint U.S.-Colombian strikes remained an option, Restrepo appeared to narrow the scope of direct American involvement.
"The United States helps us on security, helps us information, helps us on technology, but the public forces of Colombia are those who are going to act in those places," he said.
US FORCES OBLITERATE SUSPECTED 'NARCO-TERRORIST' VESSEL IN LETHAL EASTERN PACIFIC STRIKE, KILLING 3

Colombian president Abelardo De La Espriella takes part during an event announcing the new military chiefs for his government at the Jose Maria Cordova Military Cadets Academy in Bogota, Colombia August 26, 2026. (Sebastian Barros/Long Visual Press/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)
Asked specifically whether Colombia would have the "boots on the ground," Restrepo replied: "We will have our group, our public forces on the ground."

The tougher posture comes as Colombia confronts renewed violence from armed and drug-trafficking groups. This week, De La Espriella ordered the military into Santa Marta after the Autodefensas Conquistadoras de la Sierra Nevada, an illegal armed group involved in drug trafficking, responded to the killing of one of its senior leaders with an "armed strike," threats, roadblocks and attacks that left businesses shuttered and public transportation disrupted. More than 500 soldiers and 600 police officers were deployed, according to the Colombian presidency.

The new government is also seeking to reverse former President Gustavo Petro’s "total peace" policy, which pursued negotiations with several armed organizations. Before taking office, De La Espriella announced that he would dismantle key elements of the policy and reactivate arrest warrants against members of illegal armed groups.
Restrepo went further, accusing the former government of creating "the idea of impunity" and saying the new administration instead intends to confront groups it considers terrorists.
US, SHIELD OF THE AMERICAS CONDEMN 'ONGOING EFFORTS' TO OVERTHROW BOLIVIA'S ELECTED PRESIDENT AMID UNREST

Firefighters extinguish a fire in a burnt truck following a military operation by the Colombian Army against the drug-related armed group Conquering Self Defense Forces of the Sierra Nevada (ACSN) in Santa Marta, Colombia on September 22, 2026. Colombia's President Abelardo de la Espriella sent troops into Santa Marta after an armed group attacked shops and burnt vehicles across the Caribbean city, he announced on September 22, 2026. The chaos followed an earlier announcement by the president that authorities had killed 13 members of the self-styled Conquering Self Defense Forces of the Sierra Nevada (ACSN), an armed group which controls cocaine trafficking routes. (Idinael Fernandez / AFP via Getty Images)

He said that when the new government took office, "around 30%" of Colombia’s regions lacked effective territorial control — a figure Fox News Digital has not independently verified — and said the administration was seeking to regain those areas through stronger security forces, intelligence gathering, drug eradication and extraditions.

Restrepo also argued that the same security debate should extend to the United Nations, where Colombia used its General Assembly address this week to call for reforms and an international definition of terrorism. The UN has had a global counterterrorism strategy since 2006, but member states have for decades failed to agree on a comprehensive international convention defining terrorism.
Colombia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Thursday also announced that the country was suspending all diplomatic relations with Iran.

"This sovereign decision aligns with the pillars guiding the Government's foreign policy regarding national and hemispheric security, as well as the fight against transnational crime, taking into account alleged links between the Iranian government and international terrorist groups and other narcoterrorist groups that threaten the country's security," the Ministry wrote in a statement posted to X.
MELANIA TRUMP’S HOME-COUNTRY LEADER RIPS UN ‘DOUBLE STANDARDS’ AS TRUMP PROMISE IS REVEALED

Colombian Vice President Jose Manuel Restrepo attends a Shield of the Americas event on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York City, US, September 22, 2026. (Kylie Cooper/Reuters)

"I think this is a moment in which the United Nations have to reflect on its own future," Restrepo told Fox News Digital, calling for greater efficiency and effectiveness as well as international agreement on terrorism.

"The only way to attain peace, which is one of the main objectives of the UN, is through confronting terrorism," he said, arguing that countries need greater intelligence sharing, judicial cooperation and coordination.
With Secretary-General António Guterres set to leave office at the end of the year, Restrepo said the transition could offer the institution an opportunity to change.
"I think that the UN has a new moment and the UN has to take advantage of that opportunity," he said.
Restrepo added that the institution also needed to address what he described as the inconsistent application of human rights standards.

Officials shared a video showing what appeared to be various weapons laid out on a table. (@FuerzasMilCol/X)
"Human rights should apply to all, regardless of political considerations," Restrepo said. "Ideology cannot decide to whom we are going to apply or not human rights."

Efrat (Effie) Lachter is a reporter for Fox News Digital with more than 15 years of experience covering conflict, global affairs, human rights and political accountability. She has directed and produced more than 200 documentary segments across more than 40 countries, documenting conflicts, humanitarian crises, corruption, human trafficking, gender-based violence and the human stories behind major world events.

Lachter’s reporting has taken her into conflict zones and crisis areas across the Middle East, Europe, Asia and Africa. Her work has included uncovering human trafficking networks, revealing an ISIS underground torture prison in Syria, documenting the war in Ukraine and interviewing senior political figures and world leaders. She was also among the Western journalists who entered Russia after the war began to bring testimonies from Putin’s opposition. Lachter is the recipient of the 2022 Peres Center for Peace Award and was a 2023–2024 Knight-Wallace Journalism Fellow at the University of Michigan. She also won two Rockower Awards for Excellence in Reporting. She holds a bachelor's degree in communication and a master's degree in political science.

title: Fighter jet pilots eject moments before fiery crash in Wales
summary: Video captures two Royal Air Force pilots ejecting from a Hawk T2 training jet moments before a fiery crash near Anglesey in Wales on Wednesday.
story: Video captures moment two Royal Air Force pilots ejected from a training aircraft before a fiery crash in Wales. (Credit: Danni Jones via Storyful)
A video captured the moment two Royal Air Force pilots ejected from a training aircraft before a fiery crash in Wales.
The Royal Air Force (RAF) said the incident involving a Hawk T2 aircraft happened near Anglesey on Wednesday after the pilots departed the RAF Valley base in the northwestern part of the country.

"Both pilots are doing well, they are in extremely good spirits and expected to make a full recovery," the RAF said in a statement. "A formal investigation into the circumstances surrounding the incident is now underway and as a precautionary measure, the RAF has temporarily paused Hawk T1 and Hawk T2 flying operations."
BLOODIED, EJECTED MARINE CORPS PILOT SEEN CALM AND COLLECTED AFTER WASHINGTON CRASH DESTROYS AIRCRAFT
A Royal Air Force Hawk T2 training aircraft crashed in Wales on Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026. (Danni Jones via Storyful)
Footage taken by local resident Danni Jones and obtained by Storyful shows the pilots parachuting through the air after a fireball erupted in the Welsh countryside.
The RAF said on its website that the Hawk T2 "is a high-performance, 2-seat training jet equipped with advanced avionics and synthetic radar to simulate front-line combat aircraft like the Typhoon."
PILOT EJECTS AS F-35 CRASHES AT MCAS MIRAMAR, SPARKING FIRE
The Royal Air Force BAE Systems Hawk T2 is seen at RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, England, on July 20, 2024. (NurPhoto via Getty Images)
"Used primarily by the RAF for advanced jet training, it prepares pilots for complex tactical environments," it added.
The cause of Wednesday's crash was not immediately clear.
A Royal Air Force British Aerospace Hawk T2 flies along the Machynlleth Loop, a set of valleys in north Wales where pilots train in low-level flying, on March 27, 2023. (AFP via Getty Images)

"RAF Valley on Anglesey is home to No 4 Flying Training School, responsible for training the UK's next generation of world-class fighter pilots," according to the RAF. "Aircrew are also trained at RAF Valley for mountain and maritime operations throughout the world."
Greg Norman is a reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: Pope Leo XIV begins historic 4-day visit to France
summary: Pope Leo XIV's historic France visit includes a private meeting with abuse victims in Lourdes and a Saturday Mass expecting up to 1 million people.
story: Pope Leo arrived in France on Friday, Sept. 25, starting a four-day tour across Paris, Lourdes, and Metz that includes speeches and a massive outdoor mass. (HOST BROADCASTER via Reuters.)

Pope Leo XIV began his visit to France on Friday for his fifth Apostolic Journey as Pontiff. The four-day trip marks the first formal papal visit to the country once called "the eldest daughter of the Church" since Pope Benedict XVI’s visit in September 2008.

French bishops announced the visit’s theme as "That the world may have life," and it comes as the officially secular nation is seeing an influx of new baptisms. So far this year, according to the Conference of Bishops of France, more than 21,000 adults have joined the Church, an increase driven by 18 to 25-year-olds.

"Pope Leo's visit to France has sparked a real tidal wave" of interest, retired French Bishop Marc Stenger told Reuters. "French Catholics are… saying ​loudly that they need the Church to find their way in these uncertain moments in world history."
POPE LEO WARNS AI RISKS BECOMING TOOL OF 'DOMINATION, EXCLUSION AND DEATH' IN NEW ENCYCLICAL

The pope will visit Metz on Sept. 28, 2026 to conclude his four-day state and pastoral trip to France, which also includes stops in Paris and Lourdes. (Jean-Christophe Verhaegen / AFP via Getty Images)

The rise comes after a 2021 report found that some 330,000 French children had been abused by Catholic clergy and lay leaders over seven decades, and said the Church had shown "deep, total and even cruel indifference" ​to victims. Stenger, who led the Diocese of Troyes from 1999 to 2020, told Reuters the scandals "have deeply wounded the Church and damaged its credibility."
In what is described as an unusual move, the Vatican press office announced Pope Leo will meet privately in Lourdes with seven of those victims as part of a message of healing and vulnerability.
SAN FRANCISCO ARCHDIOCESE AGREES TO $395M SETTLEMENT WITH 530 CLERGY ABUSE SURVIVORS

The Vatican calls the trip, "a journey that unites faith and public engagement, memory and the future, with listening and bridge-building at its heart." After being greeted by French President Emmanuel Macron and a courtesy visit to Élysée Palace on Friday, Pope Leo is scheduled to make 15 speeches during his visit. He is expected to speak on several spiritual and societal themes, including the need to protect immigrants, the sick and unborn, and defend human dignity in the era of AI, and address themes of peace, culture, and unity.
President of France Emmanuel Macron and First Lady Brigitte Macron welcome Pope Leo XIV to Élysée Palace on Sept. 25, 2026 in Paris, France.  (Tom Nicholson/Getty Images)

French bishops have expressed surprise at the level of interest in the visit. The Associated Press reports organizers for Pope Leo’s Saturday Mass at Paris’ Place de la Concorde, expecting up to 1 million people, have lengthened the security perimeter, extending the site beyond the 1.2-mile length of the Champs-Élysées, where Pope Leo will parade in the Popemobile.

Among his more noteworthy stops, Pope Leo will worship and speak on Sunday at the Sanctuary of Our Lady of Lourdes, one of Christianity’s most-visited pilgrimage destinations, especially popular with the sick. It is where an ailing Pope John Paul II, on his final foreign trip in 2004, delivered a forceful condemnation of abortion and euthanasia.
Pope Leo XIV attends the Welcome Ceremony at Paris Orly International Airport on Sept. 25, 2026 in Paris, France.  (Simone Risoluti - Vatican Media via Vatican Pool/Getty Images)

Pope Leo’s visit, however, comes after France’s recent national debate and subsequent passage of legislation allowing adults with incurable illnesses to receive lethal medication. That followed 2024 legislation enshrining abortion as a constitutional right.
POPE LEO PROMOTES ARCHBISHOP WHO BARRED PELOSI FROM COMMUNION TO ONE OF VATICAN'S HIGHEST COURTS

On Friday, Pope Leo will speak at the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization, or UNESCO, headquarters in Paris. Vatican spokesman Matteo Bruni says Leo will likely reiterate his call for an AI slowdown and speak "with regard to the meaning of existence, to what makes human beings human and what does not."

The speech comes after the Pope’s May manifesto in which Leo warned of the dangers of AI and urged international regulation of the industry. His position again puts him at odds with President Trump, who has encouraged AI innovation so the U.S. can compete with and surpass China.

A crucifix stands in front of the Basilique Notre-Dame du Rosaire, its spire draped with a banner marking the upcoming visit of Pope Leo XIV, five days ahead of the pontiff's trip to the site as part of his apostolic journey to France, in Lourdes on Sept. 22, 2026.

Following his UNESCO visit, Pope Leo holds a prayer service at the newly-restored Cathedral of Notre-Dame, marking the first papal visit since a 2019 fire nearly destroyed one of France’s national landmarks.

He concludes his trip on Monday with a symbolic full-day visit to the border city of Metz, the birthplace of former French Prime Minister Robert Schuman, considered one of the founding fathers of the European Union. It is a backdrop the Vatican says the Pope will use to "champion friendship among European peoples."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

French Ambassador to the Vatican Charles Personnaz told Reuters that Macron has invited leaders from all 27 EU members to attend the speech and meet with the Pontiff. Other media reports say Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy may also attend.
Reuters and The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Tyler Speicher is an American journalist living in Slovenia after spending 25 years covering stories ranging from the Little League World Series to hurricanes, 9/11 and its aftermath for New York City news outlets, including 20 years on the Fox News Channel assignment desk.

title: Iranian president blames US for Middle East conflict while denying nuclear ambitions, offers to dilute uranium
summary: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian claims Tehran will submit its nuclear program to verification and dilute enriched uranium to ease tensions.
story: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian says his country will continue to resist military and economic pressure and insists the regime isn’t pursuing nuclear weapons on ‘Special Report.’

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian flatly denied Thursday that Tehran wants a nuclear bomb while claiming Iran is willing to submit its nuclear program for international inspection, blaming Washington for the nearly seven-month war in the Middle East and accusing it of blocking diplomacy.
Pezeshkian also provided fresh details about a roughly seven-hour meeting with Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei that he said took place more than a month ago.
Asked point-blank during an exclusive interview on Fox News’ "Special Report," "Do you want a nuclear bomb or not?" the Iranian leader firmly rejected the premise.

"Not at all. Not at all. Our martyred, esteemed supreme leader had announced several times that, from a religious decree, it is unholy. It is illegal," he told Bret Baier, referencing religious edicts issued against weapons of mass destruction.
IRAN 'ALREADY AGREED' TO GIVING UP NUCLEAR WEAPON AMBITIONS, TRUMP REVEALS
President Masoud Pezeshkian spoke to Bret Baier on "Special Report" (Fox News )
Pezeshkian's public denial came amid long-term international scrutiny of Iran’s nuclear program and its enrichment of uranium to levels well beyond those typically used for civilian nuclear power.
This became President Donald Trump's central rationale for launching Operation Epic Fury in February.
On Thursday, however, Pezeshkian indicated Tehran would be open to lowering its enrichment levels and allowing outside verification as part of an effort to ease nuclear tensions.
"So, that weapon's mass destruction. We said we’re willing to dilute them. It’s not a big deal. We are willing to submit ourselves to verification," he said.

Pezeshkian also pointed to the failed memorandum of understanding, or MOU, signed by him and President Donald Trump in June intended to halt hostilities and establish a framework for a broader U.S.-Iran agreement.
The process was intended by Washington to lead to an end to Iran’s nuclear ambitions and included a 60-day process toward that final deal.
"We have no problems. We did reach an agreement with your president," Pezeshkian said of Trump, who signed the document at the Palace of Versailles in France.
"That agreement was signed, and, based on that, we are willing and still wish to move forward.
IRAN NUCLEAR DEAL HINGES ON IAEA ACCESS TO LONG-BLOCKED ATOMIC WEAPON SITES, EXPERTS SAY
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and President Donald Trump (Majid Saeedi/Getty Images; Jose Luis Magana/AP)
"And the framework was agreed upon. We had not closed the Strait of Hormuz; it was open without any legal justification or framework," he assured.
"They attacked us. They assassinated and martyred our esteemed supreme leader, our scientists, our military commanders and government."
Pezeshkian then criticized Washington for the subsequent breakdown in diplomacy but insisted Tehran remains prepared to reach an agreement.
"The problem is that America, instead of conducting dialog, they descend into the arena by bombing us first, by blocking every pathway. We are ready," he said.
"This is not the way to conduct yourself on the world stage. They can have free access to see whatever we have, but not to put us under such pressure, under blockades, deny us access."
Pezeshkian also broadened his criticism of Washington, blaming the U.S. for the conflict while portraying Iran’s actions as defensive.
"We do not seek to kill Americans, as shown by actions, demonstrable actions. America has sought to kill Iranians," he said. "What we know is that if we’re attacked, we must defend ourselves."
TRUMP BETS ECONOMIC PRESSURE CAN SQUEEZE IRAN AS REGIME’S OWN FAILURES DEEPEN THE PAIN

This satellite image provided by Maxar Technologies shows a view of the Isfahan nuclear site in Iran June 22, 2025, after U.S. strikes ordered by President Donald Trump. (Joe McNally/Getty Images; Maxar Technologies via AP)
Addressing U.S. military strikes — including Operation Outcast — and increasing secondary sanctions, Pezeshkian said Iran would continue resisting Washington’s campaign.
"This is something that has been the doing of the United States," he said. "We will keep resisting. We will find ways, and the life of our country will continue. We will remain.
"Yes, we do have economic issues, certainly. But in order to remain, we will go through any hardship and endure.

"If America thinks that they can keep sanctioning us, we have nothing to do, nor do we consider any type of American elections. If the current American government, within international legal frameworks, wishes to reach an agreement, fine. If not, before the elections or after the elections, what difference does it make for us?"
Pezeshkian repeated that Iran does not want the war to continue, while blaming Israel for helping provoke the conflict and putting responsibility on Washington to bring it to an end.
TRUMP GIVES EVERY NATION AN EASY CHOICE: DO BUSINESS WITH AMERICA OR TERRORIST IRAN
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, speaks during a gathering of public relations officials in Tehran in May 2026. (Foad Ashtari/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)
"We will stand resolutely to defend ourselves. We never sought war. We do not seek war," he said.
"I deeply believe that humans should not cause the death of another human. But with the instigations conducted by Israel, they have imposed this war on us.
"But we do not wish to continue. It’s America that must choose whether it wants to end this or not."

During the interview, Pezeshkian also pointed to a roughly seven-hour, face-to-face meeting with Mojtaba Khamenei as evidence that the son of former Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei remained in charge of Iran.
"We met for about seven hours," he said. "As I said earlier, we conducted talks face to face," he added.
Addressing Khamenei’s health and whether he remained firmly in charge, Pezeshkian said: "Very much so, completely."
"The implementation of the policies is in the hands of the administration and the government. But the consultations and the directions come from there," he confirmed.
TRUMP SAYS IRAN WILL PAY — WHAT IT TAKES TO END THE WAR REMAINS UNCLEAR
Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei. (Fox News)
When Baier pressed Pezeshkian on whether Khamenei would address the Iranian people about the war or speak directly with Trump, he pointed to security concerns.
"Well, this is a process that was created in our society, which is the lack of security that was created by the action of foreigners, the action of aggressors," Pezeshkian said.

The Iranian president also addressed reports that Iranian forces used Chinese satellite imagery to carry out a deadly strike on a U.S. base in Jordan. The attack resulted in the deaths of three U.S. service members.
When questioned about the reports, Pezeshkian denied direct knowledge.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"I’m specifically unaware of these purported images that you talk about," Pezeshkian said.
"Now, what do militaries do with one another between two countries? It is their own business within their own guidelines."

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

title: Reporter's Notebook: Call for a free Iran echoes at the United Nations
summary: Retired Gen. Keith Kellogg and Ambassador Marc Ginsberg called for Iran sanctions at a rally outside the U.N. General Assembly protesting the Iranian president.
story: Fox News senior correspondent Eric Shawn reports on Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian's United Nations General Assembly speech, the U.S. delegation walkout and anti-regime protests outside U.N. headquarters on 'The Story.'
UNITED NATIONS, N.Y. — When Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian addressed the United Nations General Assembly, he portrayed his nation as the victim of American and Israeli terrorism.
But outside the hall, several thousand protesters chanted that he should be arrested for being a terrorist.
"They are terrorists. They must go!" the crowd repeatedly shouted, waving green, white and red flags of the resistance.
THE TOP MOMENTS FROM IRAN PRESIDENT’S TENSE VISIT TO US SOIL AS WAR RAGES
Demonstrators lined up outside the United Nations General Assembly Monday, Sept. 21, with flags and signs. (Brooke Curto/Fox News Digital)
"The president of Iran speaks and lies over and over again. He is a murderer. He is a terrorist," former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani told the gathering.
"It is useless to negotiate with them because they are terrorists, murderers, possibly in some ways insane religious maniacs. This would be like trying to reach an agreement with Hitler."

Various former high-level government officials struck the same tone, slamming the radical Islamic regime they say has savagely oppressed and butchered the Iranian people for decades. Estimates say upward of 20,000 protestors who took to the streets of Iran earlier this year demanding freedom have been murdered by the government. Reports of executions of political prisoners continue each week.
Demonstrators lined up outside the United Nations General Assembly Monday, Sept. 21, with flags and signs. (Brooke Curto/Fox News Digital)

"It is time now to free Iran from the mullahs," Retired Lt. General Keith Kellogg, who has served in both Trump administrations, told the gathering, "You have a road map to a secular, non-nuclear Republic of Iran, one that rejoins the free world as a friend."
TRUMP TO ZERO-IN ON IRAN NUCLEAR THREAT, GAZA PLAN AND UN OVERHAUL IN WORLD STAGE SPEECH

Former U.S. Ambassador Marc Ginsberg urged Congress to pass the Maximum Support Act, legislation that would crack down on Iran's resources, confiscate assets of the government and support internet freedom so the Iranian people could organize and have a voice.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian speaks as he holds a picture of Ali Khamenei, former supreme leader of Iran, during the 81st United Nations General Assembly at the United Nations Headquarters in New York Sept. 23, 2026. (Timothy A. Clary/AFP via Getty Images)

"All you have to do, President Trump, is to provide the funding and the support that we need, the tools the Iranian people need," Ginsberg said. "That is the type of help you promised. That is the type of help you can still provide and bring the United States closer to this exit ramp from this war and to accelerate our speed as Iran's arsenal of democracy."

"The people of Iran have rejected every form of dictatorship, whether religious or monarchical," Maryam Rajavi said in a video message to the rally. She is president-elect of the group that sponsored the protest, the National Council of Resistance of Iran.

"The voice of protest from Iran's oppressed people is being heard. The voice rejects the continued occupation of Iran's seat by religious fanatics," she said, referring to the regime's membership in the world body.
US-BACKED ISRAEL-MOROCCO DEAL DEEPENS ABRAHAM ACCORDS AMID GROWING REGIONAL THREATS
Iranians gather while blocking a street during a protest in Tehran, Iran, Jan. 9, 2026.   (MAHSA/Middle East Images/AFP via Getty Images)
The rally was held over a two-day period, and the message to the United Nations diplomats remained consistent.

"The regime only responds to firmness and decisiveness. And that's why sanctions and putting pressure on Iran has been the only solution in terms of external pressure," Alireza Jafarzadeh, deputy director of the NCRI Washington, D.C., office told Fox News.
People hold up posters of Iranian President Ebrahim Raisi during a mourning ceremony for him at Vali-e-Asr square in downtown Tehran, Iran. (AP Photo/Vahid Salemi)

"The regime is incapable of reform and change. If they were able, they would have done it a long time ago. The real solution for Iran is change by the people of Iran. They can have any talks, any concessions, none of that is going to change the behavior of the regime.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"The real Iran is represented by the people of Iran," he added. "The real change has to come from within."

Eric Shawn, a New York-based anchor and senior correspondent for FOX News Channel (FNC), joined the network when it launched in 1996. He is currently the co-anchor of FOX News Live. Shawn is also the host of Riddle: The Search for James R. Hoffa on FOX Nation, FNC's on-demand subscription-based streaming service, which is based upon his extensive reporting into the appearance of notorious Teamsters boss Jimmy Hoffa.

title: Saudi foreign minister warns Houthi threat goes global as Trump holds fire
summary: Saudi Arabia intercepted six Houthi ballistic missiles as Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud urged global action to protect Red Sea shipping routes.
story: Prince Faisal bin Farhan tells Fox News Digital that Saudi Arabia is working with the US and international partners to counter Houthi attacks and protect critical Red Sea shipping routes.

UNITED NATIONS — Saudi Arabia's foreign minister warned Thursday that the growing threat from Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis extends far beyond his country's borders, calling for international cooperation to protect critical shipping routes after Saudi forces intercepted six ballistic missiles launched toward the kingdom.

Speaking to reporters on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York, Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud told Fox News Digital that Riyadh was coordinating with Washington and other international partners as Houthi attacks threatened Saudi territory and commercial shipping in the Red Sea.

The Saudi-led coalition said Thursday that its air defenses had intercepted six ballistic missiles allegedly launched by the Houthis toward the Saudi cities of Taif and Yanbu, according to Reuters. It was not immediately clear whether the attacks caused casualties or damage.
AMERICANS WARNED AGAIN TO RETHINK TRAVEL AS MISSILE ATTACK RATTLES HISTORIC REGION

Saudi Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan Al-Saud and French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot, co-chairs of a United Nations high-level international conference hosted by France and Saudi Arabia to work towards a two-state solution between Israel and the Palestinians, listen to a question during a press briefing at U.N. headquarters in New York City, July 28, 2025. (REUTERS/Kylie Cooper)

Saudi authorities also issued emergency warnings across several areas, including Jeddah and Mecca, before announcing that the immediate danger had passed. Yanbu, a major Red Sea oil export hub, has become particularly important as the war with Iran disrupts shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

Asked by Fox News Digital whether Saudi Arabia was receiving the support it needed from the US following reports that President Donald Trump had declined Saudi requests for direct military intervention against the Houthis, Prince Faisal emphasized the kingdom's ability to defend itself while calling for a broader international response.

"So we are, of course, defending ourselves. And we are responding as necessary to the attacks by the Houthis. But we are also, of course, coordinating with all of our international allies, because this is not just about Saudi Arabia," he said.
IRAN’S PROXY MONEY MACHINE: HOW THE HOUTHIS BUILT A MULTIBILLION-DOLLAR NETWORK DESPITE US SANCTIONS

Satellite imagery shows Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key shipping waterway and the gateway to the Red Sea, as Iran threatens using Yemen's Houthi allies to shut the Bab el-Mandeb gateway to the Red Sea, in this handout picture dated July 12, 2026. (Nasa Worldview/Handout via Reuters)

"The fact that the Houthis are threatening the Bab el-Mandeb, threatening international shipping, is a risk to international security stability. That means that the responsibility to dealing with this threat is not just on Saudi Arabia, it is also on the whole international community."
The foreign minister thanked countries already working with Riyadh and confirmed that discussions with Washington were continuing.
"And we are obviously continuing to work with our partners in the U.S., to address the issue of this conflict as well," he said.
HOUTHIS ENTER US 'KILL BOX' AFTER SEIZING RED SEA 'CORK,' FORMER PENTAGON OFFICIAL WARNS

Yemen's Iran-backed armed Houthi group has warned they will move to shutter the Bab Al-Mandeb Strait through missile-drone attacks if Gulf nations join the US-Israel war on Iran. (Mohammed Hamoud/Getty Images)
His remarks came as the Trump administration faced renewed requests from Saudi Arabia to take military action against the Houthis.

According to a Sept. 21 Axios report, Trump considered ordering strikes against the group over the weekend but ultimately decided against them. The report said Saudi officials had again sought American military assistance as Houthi forces advanced in Yemen, while the U.S. continued providing intelligence and targeting support without directly entering the fighting.

The Houthis' territorial advances have intensified concerns over control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a strategic passage connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and a crucial route for international trade and Saudi oil exports.

title: Foreign leader on Putin’s doorstep sounds alarm over Iran fueling Moscow’s war machine
summary: Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs says Iran's drone tech helped Russia wage war in Ukraine as Latvia prepares to join a Strait of Hormuz coalition.
story: President Edgars Rinkēvičs tells Fox News Digital Latvia has made a political decision to support a U.S.-led coalition in the Middle East, while warning that Russia's hybrid attacks against Europe are intensifying.

UNITED NATIONS — Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs warned Wednesday that military cooperation between Russia and Iran poses a growing security concern, telling Fox News Digital in an on-camera interview that Iranian drone technology has helped Moscow wage war in Ukraine as Latvia prepares to contribute to a U.S.-led effort in the Strait of Hormuz.

Speaking on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly, Rinkēvičs said Latvia, a country of approximately 1.84 million and still a core member of NATO's eastern flank, has already made the political decision to send military specialists to support international operations in the Middle East in response to President Donald Trump's request for European assistance.

"Yes, I am concerned. Actually, we have already seen Iran helping Russia a lot, especially at the very beginning of Russia's aggression against Ukraine," Rinkēvičs said when asked about the growing cooperation between Moscow and Tehran.
PUTIN AND IRAN 'NEED EACH OTHER DESPERATELY,' EXPERT SAYS, AS RUSSIA VOICES SUPPORT FOR REGIME
Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs speaks with reporters during U.N. General Assembly High-Level Week in New York City. (Brooke Curto/Fox News Digital)

"The first drones Iranian made, or Iranian-designed drones, were used by Russia. Now Russians are actually modernizing them, making completely new technologies. But, actually, the design is still Iranian."

Earlier this week, Fox News Digital revealed documents obtained from the Russian Foreign Ministry detailing a roadmap between Russia and Iran for cooperation between 2024-2026 in multiple fields, including nuclear, finance and aviation, as well as infrastructure.

Asked whether Europe should take a more active role in countering Iran's military activities and respond to Trump's call for support, Rinkēvičs confirmed that Latvia has already taken steps toward joining an international effort in the Strait of Hormuz.
BATTLE-TESTED ZELENSKYY SOUNDS CHILLING ALARM ON WHERE PUTIN’S WAR COULD HEAD NEXT
Soldiers walk along a road near a training range in Pabradė, north of the capital Vilnius, Lithuania, March 27, 2025. (AP Photo/Mindaugas Kulbis)

"From our side, we have already made a parliamentary decision. That our EOD (explosive ordnance disposal) diver specialists could be sent to the Strait of Hormuz or to the Middle East to help out the United States, the coalition that is being formed," he said.

Rinkēvičs said Latvia hopes military activities will give way to a political solution and the restoration of global energy supplies, while expressing skepticism about the prospects for negotiations with Tehran and Moscow.
"It's very, very difficult to have diplomacy with Iran. It's very difficult with Russia," he said.

Turning to the security situation in Europe, Rinkēvičs said Latvia does not see evidence of an imminent Russian military invasion despite growing concerns about Moscow's intentions toward NATO's eastern flank.

"If Russia were able to attack us ... that would have happened already," he said. "The Russian military is not the same as it used to be back in 2022. Remember they tried to take Kyiv in three days. They are still trying to take some certain small pieces of Ukrainian territory 4½ years after the full-fledged."
IRAN’S DRONE HUNT ESCALATES AS TEHRAN TARGETS US SPY TECH TO EXPOSE BATTLEFIELD SECRETS
Iran conducts joint military exercises with Russia in the Strait of Hormuz after the U.S. deployed surveillance drones. (Iranian Army/Handout/Anadolu via Getty Images)

Explaining the immediate threat to Latvia comes instead from sabotage, cyberattacks and information campaigns, which he described as intensifying, adding that European leaders face the difficult task of preparing their populations for potential threats without creating unnecessary panic.
Rinkēvičs also warned that NATO must accelerate its adaptation to the rapidly changing nature of warfare, particularly the growing role of drones and missile technology.

While traditional military equipment, including tanks and armored personnel carriers, remains essential, the president said the war in Ukraine has demonstrated how quickly new technologies are transforming the battlefield.

The president welcomed increased NATO defense spending, crediting Trump's push for greater investment, but cautioned that additional funding alone would not resolve the alliance's military readiness challenges.
"You have money, but not always you can buy the stuff immediately, or at least you can order things. And they are delivered soon enough," he said.

Rinkēvičs said he plans to meet with U.S. defense companies during his visit to the U.S., saying, "When it comes to the U.S. support, let me just say that the United States does an amazing job already. We do have U.S. troops, not big numbers, but I think sufficient numbers are now stationed in our airbase in Lielvārde.
"U.S. presence in the Baltics is very important, and we are working with our U.S. partners about further rotations."
