title: Charles Spencer’s Book, ‘Swan Song’: Biggest Takeaways About Princess Diana
summary: What’s happening with Charles Spencer’s book, Swan Song? Here’s what to know and the biggest takeaways.
story: “Catch Me Up” is a TODAY series where our experts and journalists bring readers up to speed on the day’s biggest headlines.

The brother of the late Princess Diana has reignited the British royal drama surrounding her life and death with a new book giving his side of the story on her funeral, relationship with King Charles III and more.

Charles Spencer, 62, writes in “Swan Song” that his mother once told him he knew his sister Diana “better than anyone else in the world.” His aim is to “tell the truth about Diana, from her brother’s perspective.”
The allegations and remembrances in the book about Diana’s ex-husband, King Charles III, provoked a rare public response from Buckingham Palace.

“While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and color memory in ways others do not recognize, even many years after such a loss,” Buckingham Palace officials said in a statement on Sept. 16.

Diana was one of the most famous women in the world after marrying then-Prince Charles in 1981. Their high-profile marriage ended in 1996, and she died in a car crash in 1997 after being chased by paparazzi with her boyfriend Dodi Fayed. Fayed died, as did driver Henri Paul. Only bodyguard Trevor Rees-Jones survived.
Here’s what to know about Spencer’s claims and remembrances in “Swan Song.”
Prince Charles Said ‘We’ll Soon Forget’ Diana Ahead of Her Funeral

Spencer writes that then-Prince Charles made some ugly comments amid a dispute between the Spencers and the royal family over whether Diana’s children, Prince William and Prince Harry, should walk behind her coffin at her 1997 funeral.
Spencer thought it would be “barbaric,” but was told the boys’ father, Charles, wanted them to do it. Charles then angrily called him, Spencer writes.
“That’s the problem with your family, they’ve got no bloody sense of duty!” Spencer recalled Charles saying.
He writes that Charles then paused and unleashed “his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death.”
“Rest assured,’ he hissed, ‘we’ll forget her soon enough!’” Charles said about Diana.
“I can’t believe you just said that,” Spencer recalled saying.
Spencer writes that a palace official later called him and said the boys indicated that they wanted to walk behind their mother’s coffin, which was captured in memorable photos.
He Recalls His First Conversation with Prince Charles After Diana’s Death

Spencer writes that Prince Charles sounded “giddily elated,” in contrast to other callers, “who were stunned, barely able to articulate their condolences and offers of help.” Spencer remembers thinking his former brother-in-law sounded like a “lottery winner.”

“Looking back now, I suspect the prince’s first reaction must have been to think more of how this event might free him to marry the woman he loved, rather than appreciating the loss of one he did not. It can be hard to feel too much sympathy for an ex-spouse, or those who care for them profoundly, after bitter divorce,” he writes.
Charles went on to marry Camilla Parker Bowles, now Queen Camilla. Charles, in a 1994 interview, admitted to being unfaithful in his marriage to Diana.
Prince Charles Was Cruel to Diana About Her Weight and His Feelings For Her
Diana’s insecurities and body image issues were exacerbated by Charles, according to the book.
Spencer writes that just days after her engagement to the British royal in February 1981, Charles squeezed her waist and said, ‘Oh, a bit chubby here, aren’t we?”

He says his sister told him her waist shrank 5½ inches between her engagement and wedding. She confided in him that she had been suffering from an eating disorder for five months by her wedding day. The disorder was brought on by seeing her engagement photos.
Spencer later writes that Diana confided to a friend that Charles had told her “he was very happy to marry her, but he was not actually in love with her.”
Diana Said Charles Was ‘In Love With His Valet’
In a chapter about how Diana informed her brother that she was getting divorced from Charles, he tells her he fears the public will vilify her for ruining the fantasy of the royal marriage.
“But, Carlos, my husband is in love with his valet,’” he said Diana replied.
The valet is not specifically named. Spencer said he gulped in response.
“Well, I guess in that case, you don’t really have a choice,” he replied.
Diana Expressed Doubts About Her Wedding to Charles
Spencer recalls hearing that Diana went to their father, John Spencer, and said “she could not go through with marriage to a man who clearly did not love her.”
He said their father was “appalled” and “said it was impossible to pull out of such an enormous commitment at that point.”
Spencer described a subsequent birthday party for then-Prince Andrew in which Diana looked forward to reuniting with Prince Charles.
“But he had shown next to no interest in her, and she — deeply hurt, confused and increasingly concerned — danced with others, including me, instead,” he writes.
Charles Ranted About Queen Elizabeth II and Prince Philip Treating Him ‘Like a Child’
Spencer writes that he and Charles were standing “awkwardly” after the funeral for Spencer’s father when Charles blurted out, “You’re so lucky! You know, inheriting when you’re so young!”
Spencer writes that he had no idea how to react, as he was devastated by his father’s loss. Charles then expounded on his comment.

“You’re inheriting this place in your 20s. And, I mean, I’m 43,’ he said, ‘and I employ 50 people’ – he was flushed in the face now – ‘but my parents insist on treating me like – like a child!’ At this he stamped his foot in emphasis, I have to say, very much like a child; and a petulant one, at that.”
Diana Pushed Her Stepmother Down a Staircase
Spencer writes that he and his sister both “hated” their stepmother, Raine Spencer, whom their father, John Spencer, married in 1976.
Diana was “outraged” when she found out her father married Raine, while Charles considered her “a gold-digger.”

Diana’s dislike for her stepmother boiled over into a physical confrontation, according to the book. He said the two were at the top of a staircase in Althorp, home of the Spencer family, when Raine made a cutting remark.
“I have always felt so very sorry for the Prince of Wales, marrying somebody quite as stupid as you,” Raine said, according to Spencer.
Diana then “took a step forward, hooked a long leg round Raine’s calves before shoving her down the carpeted staircase.”
Spencer writes that his stepmother landed on her backside, got up, and left without a glance.
Spencer also writes that despite their fraught relationship for years, Diana and Raine seemed to form a “genuine friendship.”

title: ‘A Different World’ Stars Reveal the Surprising Romances That Happened Off Screen
summary: “A Different World” stars Cree Summer, Darryl M. Bell and Jasmine Guy remember Summer dating co-star Kadeem Hardison during the show’s run.
story: Viewers loved the romance between Whitley and Dwayne on “A Different World,” but it’s what was going on when the cameras weren’t rolling that may surprise fans.

Show stars Jasmine Guy, Cree Summer and Darryl M. Bell stopped by TODAY with Jenna & Sheinelle on Sept. 23 to talk about the new Netflix reboot and reminisce about their time shooting the original sitcom, which included dishing about the real-life relationship happening off-camera.

“Whitley and Dwayne were that iconic couple that we all wanted to be, but we truly believe that you guys were dating,” guest co-host Justin Sylvester asked Guy of her co-star Kadeem Hardison. “You couldn’t tell me that that wasn’t real love. Was it behind the scenes? Did you guys have a little something something?”
“I do really love him, but he was seeing her,” Guy replied, pointing to Summer.
“In real life?” asked Sheinelle Jones. “You guys were dating? Why was I today years old when I found that out?”
Hardison, who plays Dwayne Wayne, and Summer dated while filming the show. Meanwhile, on-screen, Summer’s character, Freddie, started dating Ron Johnson, played by Bell, in Season 6.
“So I’m kissing Kadeem’s best friend,” Summer said, pointing to Bell.
“And Kadeem is kissing my best friend,” she added, pointing to Guy.
“Oh, that is just funny,” Sheinelle said.
“Very incestuous,” Summer added.
“Quite incestuous, yes,” said Guy.

The strangeness of the situation didn’t end there, though. Turns out, Guy’s boyfriend at the time, Dominic Hoffman, appeared in “A Different World” as one of Whitley’s love interests, Julian, who had a recurring role in the third and fourth seasons.
“Oh, it was messy over at Hillman!” Sylvester joked.
“It sounds very ‘Brady Bunch’-y,” Guy quipped.

“A Different World” aired for six seasons on NBC from 1987 until 1993. Enrollment at HBCUs increased more than 25% between 1976 and 1994, but the largest jump occurred between 1986 and 1994, according to the National Center for Education Statistics. That eight-year period is in lockstep with the show’s run.

“Every day, just like this, every day, one of us, someone will come and say, ‘I went to an HBCU because I watched “A Different World,”’ or ‘I went to college because I watched “A Different World.”’ ‘I’m a doctor,’ ‘I’m a lawyer,’ ‘I’m an engineer because I watched “A Different World,”’ Bell said.
“And then they’re like, ‘I found my Whitley or my Dwayne from “A Different World,”’ he continued. “It’s the gift that keeps on giving to us.”
The reboot of “A Different World” premieres on Netflix on Sept. 24, exactly 39 years to the day after the original comedy premiered on NBC.

title: Jon Hamm Opens Up About Becoming a Dad on TODAY, Including the 1 Thing He’s Most Excited About
summary: Jon Hamm and wife Anna Osceola are expecting their first child. The “Your Friends & Neighbors” co-stars married in June 2023.
story: Jon Hamm and wife Anna Osceola now have one additional outfit for their little one.

The former “Mad Men” star appeared on TODAY Sept. 23 to talk about his new series “American Hostage” on MGM+ in which he plays a radio host thrust into a crisis in 1977 when a hostage-taker  demands he take his call on air.
During his chat with Craig Melvin, Hamm also spoke about expecting his first child with Osceola.

“It’s great,” Hamm said. “The best thing I keep hearing is how much it changes you for the better. I’m very excited. I’ve been around kids my whole life. I’ve been a teacher, my nieces and nephews and all that stuff, so I’m excited to start our own family.
“And it’s thrilling. And terrifying.”
The couple are gathering all the essentials that their newborn will need, including plenty of onesies.
Now, they’ll have one more, as the anchors surprised Hamm with a special TODAY onesie in honor of Hamm’s professed love for Bravo programming and “The Real Housewives” franchise.
The special onesie reads, “Going to bed, so daddy can watch Bravo.”
“Beautiful,” Hamm said. “This will get used, I can tell you that much.”
Hamm also received a special message from Sonja Morgan, a former cast member of “The Real Housewives of New York City.”
The “Your Friends & Neighbors” co-stars were first rumored to be welcoming a child in August.
Hamm, 55, and Osceola, 38, tied the knot in June 2023.
The following year, Hamm opened up to The Hollywood Reporter about possibly starting a family with his new bride.
Hamm told the publication his parents’ divorce when he was young initially turned him off of the idea of marriage. But all that changed when he met Osceola.

“Obviously, my parents were not married long,” said Hamm, whose mom died when he was 10, “so I don’t have a model to look at and go, ‘Oh, this is how one finds happiness.’ I just knew at a certain point I wanted to be with this person. But when I proposed, I was terrified. I was like, ‘What am I doing?’”
The actor went on to say he and Osceola enjoyed a “perfect” wedding day in Big Sur at the same location the “Mad Men” finale was filmed nine years before.
The “emotional” event, he said, gave him “a reset, a reboot, a reframe, a reimagining.”
“So, it’s been great. And I hope it turns into kids. It’s not lost on me that I’m 53. I will be the old dad, but so it goes. It could be a good thing. We’ll see,” Hamm said.
Less than a year before getting hitched, Hamm opened up about his relationship with Osceola during a September 2022 interview on Howard Stern’s SiriusXM show.

“This is another place in my life that I feel very settled and comfortable. I’m in a relationship right now and ... it’s comfortable,” he said, adding, “It’s about taking care of someone else and being taken care of.”

Hamm revealed that after undergoing therapy to work on the “wound” of losing his mother at such a young age, he had become “opened up the possibility of things like being married, having kids, defining a new version of happiness, life, wellness.”
“It sounds hokey and whatever, but it’s real and for want of a better word, it’s what I’m working for. What else is there other than that?”

title: Frances Bean Cobain, 34, Makes Rare Red Carpet Appearance, Her First Since 2018
summary: Frances Bean Cobain made a rare public appearance when she attended a screening of the movie “The Deputy” in Los Angeles on Sept. 22.
story: Frances Bean Cobain made a rare public appearance when she attended a screening of the movie “The Deputy” in Los Angeles on Sept. 22.
It marked the first time the 34-year-old daughter of late Nirvana singer Kurt Cobain and Courtney Love had been photographed on a red carpet since 2018.
Cobain wore a brown leather jacket, which she paired with knee-high white boots, black shorts and a graphic T-shirt.
She is listed as an executive producer of “The Deputy,” according to IMDB. The film, which stars Duke Nicholson, William H. Macy and Tiffany Haddish, opens Sept. 25.

Cobain was last photographed at a public event in June 2019 when she attended the Moschino Spring/Summer 20 Menswear and Women’s Resort Collection show in Los Angeles. Her last red carpet appearance occurred at the Moschino x H&M fashion show in New York City in October 2018. Earlier that year, she was also photographed with Love at a concept store opening in Los Angeles.
Cobain and Riley Hawk, son of skateboarding legend Tony Hawk, married in October 2023, according to People. In September 2024, the couple welcomed a son named Ronin.
Cobain celebrated Ronin’s 2nd birthday earlier this month with a carousel of photos of him on Instagram.

“Happy 2nd birthday to this sweet potato fanatic, free wheeling, adrenaline seeking, nature loving, wind in the willows, sunshine boy!!” she wrote. “Once a day Riley & I look over at each other to say ‘I can’t believe we made him.’ I would live through every hard thing 1,000 times again, knowing it all lead to a present, loving life with this kid. Thank the universe he is here.”
Kurt Cobain died by suicide in 1994 when his daughter was 1. On the 30th anniversary of his death in 2024, she reflected on life without him.

“I wish I could’ve known my Dad. I wish I knew the cadence of his voice, how he liked his coffee or the way it felt to be tucked in after a bedtime story,” she wrote on Instagram. “I always wondered if he would’ve caught tadpoles with me during the muggy Washington summers, or if he smelled of Camel Lights & strawberry nesquik (his favorites, I’ve been told).

“But there is also deep wisdom being on an expedited path to understanding how precious life is. He gifted me a lesson in death that can only come through the LIVED experience of losing someone,” she continued. “It’s the gift of knowing for certain, when we love ourselves & those around us with compassion, with openness, with grace, the more meaningful our time here inherently becomes.”
She went on to reveal how she remained connected to him, decades after his death.
“Kurt wrote me a letter before I was born. The last line of it reads, ‘wherever you go or wherever I go, I will always be with you,’” she wrote.

“He kept this promise because he is present in so many ways. Whether it’s by hearing a song or through the hands we share, in those moments I get to spend a little time with my dad & he feels transcendent,” she added. “To anyone who has wondered what it would’ve looked like to live along side the people they have lost, I’m holding you in my thoughts today. The meaning of our grief is the same.”

title: Trump rolls out red carpets for Xi, though he has portrayed China as a global menace
summary: Just two months ago, President Donald Trump gave a primetime speech accusing China of interfering in the 2020 election.
story: WASHINGTON — He has accused China of hacking America’s elections and plundering its wealth, yet President Donald Trump has showered the visiting Chinese leader, Xi Jinping, with tributes and affection during their summit meeting this week at the White House.

Trump met his Chinese counterpart on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, outside Washington on Wednesday rather than wait back at the White House for an official greeting. It’s the first time he has ever shown a visiting world leader that courtesy.

Trump rolled out a red carpet not once but twice for Xi. The leaders walked side by side down a 100-foot-long red carpet after Xi’s Air China plane landed at Andrews. Another red carpet was laid out Thursday morning when Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, arrived at the White House for the summit’s first full day.
In the evening, Trump feted Xi at a state dinner whose menu included sesame-crusted sea bass and braised bok choy, followed by a dessert of vanilla crémeux and honey ice cream.

“As the leaders of our two nations, President Xi and I both understand that we represent different systems, but the ties between our people endure, and we’ve never gotten along better since the first trade ships from New York left the harbor to arrive on the banks of the Pearl River,” Trump said at the dinner.
He gave his guest a statue of a bald eagle as a gift.

All the pomp and ceremony might appear unusual given Trump’s past complaints that China has meddled in elections and exploited the U.S. through trade. Just two months ago, Trump gave a rare primetime speech asserting that China interfered in the 2020 election, which he lost to Joe Biden.
But Trump, who has long believed that personal relationships are key to managing geopolitical tensions, has set out to charm the Chinese leader.

“From the time of my first election in 2016, President Xi and I have forged a friendship — a truly great friendship, actually — built on mutual respect and the vital interests of our people,” Trump said Thursday morning in joint public statements he and Xi made before they held a private meeting in the Oval Office.
Xi struck a cordial tone in his remarks, saying he and Trump have developed a “personal rapport and stayed in touch.”

He also made an announcement certain to delight American children and anyone who has ever logged on to a panda-cam feed for a respite from life’s pressures: China will soon send two giant pandas, Ping Ping and Fu Shang, to the Atlanta zoo, Xi said.

In an unusual rebuke from a member of Trump’s own party, Sen. Roger Wicker, R-Miss., chairman of the Armed Services Committee, said Wednesday in a speech on the Senate floor that, “quite frankly, had the White House asked me for advice, I would have suggested the president not invite Xi Jinping to Washington for such a lavish welcome here in the United States of America, based on all of the troubling issues we have with President Xi and the Chinese Communist Party.”
President Trump in landmark meeting with China’s leader

China may also have aided Iran in the war with the U.S. An F-15 fighter jet that was shot down over Iran in April was most likely hit by a Chinese-made shoulder-launched missile, three people familiar with the matter told NBC News. And in the early days of the seven-month-old conflict, China may have given Iran radar capabilities to help spot stealth aircraft, according to one of the people and a U.S. official with knowledge of the matter.

Honoring the leader of the world’s largest communist country may also undercut an argument Trump has made to discredit Democrats in the midterm elections. He has warned repeatedly that Democratic candidates would steer the U.S. in a communist direction if they are elected.
Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, told NBC News on Thursday, “I personally look at the red-carpet treatment and thought it was a little bit over the top.”
Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., said in an interview that while he didn’t mind seeing Xi thrown a dinner, “I don’t think the president ought to believe his bull----.”
After the U.S. and Israel launched attacks on Iran on Feb. 28, the Iranian regime exerted a chokehold over the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial shipping lane for oil supplies.
Xi “could open up that strait with a phone call, and in a myriad of ways, he is helping Iran with military equipment, intelligence,” Kennedy said. “The guy learned to lie before he learned to talk.”
China, which has criticized the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran and called for diplomatic negotiations, denies supplying Iran with weapons or military equipment.

No substantive breakthroughs are expected at the summit, foreign policy experts said. The two presidents were set to discuss trade, the Iran war and artificial intelligence, among other issues that have divided the U.S. and China. Trump entered the summit in a weakened posture, experts said, vexed by the prolonged Iran war and looming midterm congressional elections in which his party could lose its slim majority. He lacks the leverage needed to wring concessions from China, experts said.

Mark Montgomery, a retired Navy admiral, said at a pre-summit event hosted by the FDD think tank: “We have a president entering this playing a weak hand. I’m not 100% sure President Trump knows he’s playing a weak hand. I am 100% sure that leader Xi knows Trump is playing a weak hand.”

One area of cooperation might be the creation of a hotline that the U.S. and China could use to cope with an emergency arising from rapidly evolving AI technology, Secretary of State Marco Rubio suggested in an interview on “Fox & Friends” this week.
“It’s not a bad idea; it’s one that we’ll explore with the Chinese, among others,” Rubio said.

Along with closed-door meetings, Trump made a point to show off his prized White House projects. He took Xi outside to see the helipad he built on the South Lawn. Both men pointed down at the granite base.
When the leaders passed the press corps at one point, Trump said, “We had a great meeting.” He said Xi was “an expert on stone, aside from many other things, and he loves good granite.”
Xi said nothing.

Walking with Xi along the West Wing Colonnade, Trump pointed to his “Presidential Walk of Fame” — pictures and biographical accounts of former presidents. He paused at the portrait of Biden, showing how he has mocked Biden by referring to him as “Autopen,” the device that presidents have used when they don’t have time to sign their own names to documents. A video snippet released by the White House shows the two presidents chuckling at the picture of Biden, with Trump giving Xi a friendly pat on the arm.

Confronting Xi in the moment may prove difficult for Trump. Xi is president for life; Trump is a president at risk of losing his governing majority in Congress. His approval rating has hit a second-term low.

One source of Xi’s leverage is his hold over rare earth materials, which are used in high-tech manufacturing. Last year, Trump slapped China with steep tariffs, igniting a trade war. Trump has long complained that China’s trade policies have bled the U.S. of wealth.

A statement from the White House in April 2025, tied to Trump’s “Liberation Day” tariffs, said Chinese practices “have given China global dominance in key manufacturing industries, decimating U.S. industry.”

But China’s command of rare earth supplies has proved an effective countermeasure, a resource the Trump administration can’t afford to lose. The two sides agreed to a trade truce last year, and on Wednesday they agreed to extend it two months, from Nov. 10 to Jan. 10.
Add to Google
Add to Google

Viewers who wanted to watch the summit live faced unusual difficulties following a media ban that Trump imposed last week. He barred CNN, MS NOW and Politico from entering the White House grounds, prompting them to sue to regain access.

CNN is part of the five-network press “pool” that provides real-time coverage of the president’s public events. In solidarity with CNN and the other outlets that were banned, the other networks opted to suspend video pool coverage of Trump.

Confusion reigned in the hours before Xi arrived. ABC News had been scheduled to provide the pooled video feed. A White House official hurriedly approached a network journalist and asked where the camera was. Absent any clarity over when the banned outlets’ access would be restored, ABC declined to record.

Trump took notice that TV coverage had thinned. He wrote on social media that CNN and MS NOW “refused to cover one of the Biggest and Most Beautiful Events to take place in many years, the arrival at the White House of the Highly Respected President of China, Xi Jinping, and his beautiful wife, Madam Peng.”

Journalists from both CNN and MS NOW were physically unable to cover Xi’s arrival at the White House. Though a federal judge had ruled overnight that their access must be restored, they were still barred from entering the White House until about two hours after Xi showed up.
During a photo spray with Xi later in the day, Trump joked that China had the friendliest press corps, according to a press pool report.
A Reporters Without Borders survey of press freedoms worldwide ranked China 178th out of 180 countries, sandwiched between North Korea and Iran.

title: Iran’s president says Tehran wants a deal with U.S. before midterm elections
summary: In an exchange with news organizations, Iran’s Masoud Pezeshkian also described meeting twice with the Islamic Republic’s new supreme leader, who hasn’t been seen in public.
story: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Thursday suggested his government was willing to make a deal with the U.S. to end the war before Americans head to the polls this November.
“We don’t want it to get to the midterm elections,” Pezeshkian said in a brief meeting with NBC News and other news organizations on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly.

“We wish Americans to return to the MOU before the midterms,” Pezeshkian added, referring to a memorandum of understanding between the U.S. and Iran that laid out plans for a temporary ceasefire. The agreement, signed in June, eventually collapsed.
Iran’s president strikes a defiant tone at U.N. after Trump threats

In response to NBC News’ request for comment, White House spokesperson Anna Kelly said: “The Iranian regime has murdered thousands of its own people, killed Americans overseas, executed acts of terrorism in the Strait of Hormuz, and launched indiscriminate attacks against its neighbors in the region.”
“The President is courageously ensuring that such an evil country never possesses a nuclear weapon, which will make the entire world safer and more stable,” Kelly added.

Pezeshkian’s comments came two days after President Donald Trump said in a speech to world leaders at the U.N. that he believed the Iranian regime would not make a deal to settle the conflict until after the fall elections.
“I believe we’ll make a deal right after the election because it doesn’t make sense for them not to,” Trump said. “They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election.”

Polls show Democrats with an advantage heading into the November contests. The latest NBC News Decision Desk Poll found 31% of respondents approved of Trump’s handling of the Iran war, while 69% disapproved.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told a group of reporters in a separate briefing in New York on Thursday that a plan has been presented to U.S. officials through mediators during talks this week that would lead to the opening of the Strait of Hormuz and the resumption of talks after seven days.
Araghchi said the plan could begin as soon as the U.S. agreed to it and maintained it plan did not go beyond the memorandum of understanding signed by Trump in June.

“We have introduced a plan to the United States through the intermediators that, if certain conditions are met, the Strait of Hormuz will be open at the end of seven days and talks will be restarted,” Araghchi said. “The conditions we have asked the U.S. to meet is nothing new, nothing more than what was already in the Islamabad agreement, which was signed by the U.S. president.”
Araghchi pointed out that one of the conditions of the plan is for the U.S. to accept a maritime transit route through the Strait of Hormuz that has been agreed upon by Iran and Oman.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Trump on Tuesday defended the conflict and said he was considering whether to “annihilate” the country or make a deal.

Trump has repeatedly said that the goal of attacking Iran was to prevent the development of a nuclear weapon. Soon after the war started, Iran blocked the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway through which some 20% of the world’s oil flowed before the conflict, sending shock waves through the world economy.
In the exchange with news organizations, Pezeshkian said he has met with the Islamic Republic’s new leader twice — including a month ago, for seven hours.

Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei assumed the role in early March after his father, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, was killed in an Israeli attack that also killed family members and other senior leaders.

Pezeshkian said he did not see “any issues with his health or physical appearance” in their meetings, adding that they sat on the floor on traditional pillows. Mojtaba Khamenei was severely injured in the strike that killed his father, three people with knowledge of the matter told NBC News in July, with burns to his face and body and wounds that have required several operations to one of his legs.

Iran’s president briefly addressed other pressing issues affecting the relationship between Tehran and Washington. He said his government was “open” to inspections of its nuclear facilities, which the regime has long maintained are for civilian purposes, and he insisted the regime was not seeking to assassinate the American president.
“This has not been the position of the Iranian government that we seek to assassinate President Trump or his family members,” Pezeshkian said.
Add to Google
Add to Google
The Justice Department charged an Iranian man in November in an alleged murder-for-hire effort to kill Trump when he was the Republican presidential candidate in 2024.
Two others were charged with planning to kill an Iranian American journalist and activist who has criticized the Iranian government over its treatment of women.

U.S. authorities said the plot was part of Iran’s efforts to avenge the death of a top Iranian general, Qassem Soleimani, who was killed in Baghdad in a U.S. drone strike Trump ordered during his first term in the White House.
Pezeshkian has previously denied an Iranian plot to kill Trump, telling NBC News’ Lester Holt in Tehran last year that the regime would “never” do so.

title: Netanyahu defends Iran war, calls Gaza genocide accusations a lie in defiant U.N. address
summary: As Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu pleads his country’s case at the United Nations General Assembly, his target audience will likely be Israeli voters.
story: TEL AVIV — Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu pleaded his country’s case to the world at the United Nations General Assembly on Thursday before an audience of mostly empty seats.
But the audience Netanyahu was really trying to reach was closer to home: Israeli voters ahead of next month’s crucial elections.
As Netanyahu stepped up to the lectern, hundreds of diplomats showed their disdain for Israel’s bloody crackdown on Palestinians in Gaza by rising from their seats and walking out en masse.
Netanyahu responded with similar disdain. “If there are any more moral cowards who haven’t left the hall, please do so now,” he said.
U.N. delegates walk out as Netanyahu begins his address
Then Netanyahu went on to revisit Hamas’ attacks on Israel in October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and which sparked the latest round of fighting.
Netanyahu also defended the ongoing war on Iran in existential terms. “If we hadn’t done it, we’d all be dead,” he said.
“We will continue to defend our state. We will continue to win because we have no other choice,” he said.
Netanyahu thanked President Donald Trump for taking Israel’s side in what he called a “battle against the barbarians.”
And, as expected, he accused New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani of antisemitism and cozying up to what he said were his Hamas “buddies.”
“You can’t silence me,” he said, addressing Mamdani. “You can’t silence the truth.”
Mamdani said in a statement later that Netanyahu “used his speech to repeat baseless lies meant to sanitize his genocide of Palestinians.”
“Yet no lie can change the fact that he remains the subject of an International Criminal Court arrest warrant alleging war crimes and crimes against humanity,” he said.

title: Senate rejects resolution calling to end the Iran war as most Republicans stick with Trump
summary: The same resolution passed the House in July.
story: WASHINGTON — The Senate on Thursday rejected a symbolic resolution calling for President Donald Trump to end the U.S. war with Iran, with most Republicans siding with the president despite the war’s unpopularity.
Just a handful of Republicans joined Democrats in favor of the resolution: Sens. Rand Paul of Kentucky, Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Thom Tillis of North Carolina.

But the majority of the GOP voted against the measure, including Sens. Jon Husted of Ohio and Dan Sullivan of Alaska, who are in some of the most competitive races. Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., was the only Democrat to vote no.
The final vote was 49-50.
Add to Google
Add to Google

The measure passed the House in July by a vote of 214-208. Prices on gas, diesel, fertilizer and food have all risen in the U.S. as Iran has turned the Strait of Hormuz into a war zone in retaliation against military strikes that began in February. Nineteen U.S. service members have died.

A recent NBC News poll found that just 33% of registered voters believe the Iran war was worth it, while 62% believe it was not worth it. By a margin of 57%-24%, voters are more likely to support a candidate who opposes the Iran war.

As a concurrent resolution, the measure expresses the view of Congress. Had it passed the Senate, it would not go to the president for a signature or veto, making it a largely symbolic rebuke of Trump’s ongoing war.

It stated: “Congress hereby directs the President to remove the use of United States Armed Forces from hostilities against the Islamic Republic of Iran or any part of its government or military, including potential ground forces in a combat role or used for occupation, unless explicitly authorized by a declaration of war or specific authorization for use of military force against Iran.”

While most Republicans in both chambers continue to side with Trump on the war, some candidates in competitive 2026 elections have defected amid negative public sentiment. In recent days, GOP Senate candidates like Mike Rogers in Michigan and Rep. Ashley Hinson in Iowa have called for ending the war after siding with Trump on it for months.

“It’s more than a message,” Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., said of the war powers resolution. “Congress has the constitutional power to declare war, not the president. So that’s the reason it doesn’t go to the White House, because the White House can’t veto the Constitution.”
Kaine has led the charge in the Senate to reassert Congress’ power to declare war, hoping to put pressure on Trump.

“If you don’t want to listen to us, how about listen to the American public who’s suffering? Listen to the 18 families who’ve lost loved ones,” Kaine said. “Listen to the hundreds of troops who’ve been injured. Listen to the families, the eight who tried to commit suicide in the extended appointment on the Lincoln.”
Trump has defended the war as an effort to weaken Iran and prevent the country from building a nuclear weapon.

“Just imagine such a vile regime were ever empowered to carry out large-scale terror attacks from behind a nuclear shield. This was the reality we had to confront. A reality that far too many preferred to ignore,” Trump told world leaders in a speech at the United Nations on Wednesday.

title: Pope Leo champions free press, dodges White Sox miracle question
summary: Pope Leo XIV said Friday he welcomes journalists to chronicle his travels, in sharp contrast to President Donald Trump, who recently kicked three news outlets out of the White House before having to undo that ban.
story: ABOARD THE PAPAL PLANE — Pope Leo XIV said Friday he welcomes journalists to chronicle his travels, in sharp contrast to President Donald Trump, who recently kicked three news outlets out of the White House before having to undo that ban.

The leader of the world’s Catholics was asked about the White House’s most recent bout with America’s free press — and while the pontiff didn’t mention Trump by name, he said good and thorough news coverage “is very important.”
Pope Leo is asked if he helped with historic White Sox turnaround
A federal court on Thursday forced the Trump administration to temporarily restore CNN’s, MS NOW’s and Politico’s access to their White House workspaces.

“I am very happy that here you are all welcome, and we have it all the way around for everybody,” the pope said. “Good coverage, I think, is very important, and we have it all the way around for everybody. Thank you.”

On a lighter note, the Chicago-raised Leo smiled broadly when he was asked about his beloved White Sox qualifying for the MLB playoffs — an overachievement of near-biblical proportions considering that the South Siders lost 121 games as recently as 2024.
“Some call it a miracle. Do you have anything to do with that?” a reporter asked.
“No comment,” a smiling Leo said. “Great things happen in Chicago.”

The White Sox won the 2005 World Series, and Fox television cameras caught a passing glimpse of fan Robert Prevost — the man who’d later become Cardinal Robert Francis Prevost and then the first American pope.
Claudio Lavanga reported from aboard the papal plane, and David K. Li reported from New York City.

title: Yemen says it asked Trump for U.S. military support in fight against Houthis
summary: A senior official said Yemen is seeking help as the Iranian-backed rebels tighten their grip on its Red Sea coast, threatening to further disrupt global energy shipments.
story: The government of Yemen is seeking U.S. military support in its fight against the Houthis, a senior Yemeni official said Wednesday, as the Iranian-backed rebels rapidly expand their control of Yemen’s Red Sea coast and threaten another critical Middle East waterway for global energy supplies.

Yemen’s president, Rashad al-Alimi, conveyed the request for U.S. assistance to President Donald Trump in a call this week, Abdullah Al-Alimi Bawazir, vice president of the Yemeni Leadership Council, told reporters on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly.

Asked about a report this week by Reuters, which cited one Yemeni and one Western source as saying Trump made no direct pledge of military support during the call, Bawazir said he was unaware that the request had been rejected.
He said that Trump understands the danger of the Houthis and that “we hope and expect more support for the Yemeni government in the face of the Houthi militias.”
The White House did not immediately respond to an emailed request for comment overnight.
Houthis claim attack on Saudi capital
Bawazir did not say whether U.S. support should extend to direct military strikes.
“We do not ask the American soldiers to actually go into war on our behalf,” he said. “And we don’t really request that they do nothing.”

Yemen does look forward to “mutual coordination on the intel and security fields,” according to Bawazir, who requested that the U.S. enhance the Yemeni government’s own military capacity to take on the threat.
“The aerial campaigns are important,” he said. “But supporting the Yemeni government and forces on the ground is indeed a guarantor to end the danger of those militias.”

Yemen has been embroiled in various states of conflict since 2014, when the Houthis drove the internationally recognized government out of the capital city, Sanaa, and ignited a regional proxy war, with Saudi Arabia supporting the exiled government against the Iranian-backed rebels.

In their latest military campaign, the Houthis have advanced along Yemen’s Red Sea coastline with the aim of cutting off the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which has become a critical waterway for Saudi Arabia to transport oil after Iran effectively shut down the Strait of Hormuz.

Saudi Arabia, a critical U.S. ally in the Middle East, including in the U.S. war with Iran, has urged the U.S. to take military action against the Houthis, who further escalated their actions over the weekend by launching an attack on the Saudi capital, Riyadh. So far U.S. support has been limited to providing intelligence and targeting data.

Trump, who announced a ceasefire with the Houthis last year after weeks of punishing strikes against the militant group, went so far as to order strikes against the Houthis on Sunday, NBC News has reported, but the order was canceled hours later.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Wednesday that the U.S. has made commitments to the Saudis and is living up to them, adding that “obviously, the president has many options available to him.”
Trump said this month that the Houthis, which the U.S. designates as a terrorist organization, don’t want to fight the U.S. and “they don’t want us to go after them.”

“They’ve called and they’ve talked to us, and they don’t want us to,” Trump told reporters while he was in Ireland. “They would much prefer not having us involved, and they’re letting most ships go through.”

Mohamed al-Bukhaiti, a member of the Houthis’ political bureau, told The Associated Press on Sunday that it was the U.S. that had reached out to the rebel group after its advancement toward the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
“We confirmed that we are not targeting the United States, or any other nation, in the strait, with the sole exception of the Saudi enemy,” al-Bukhaiti said. “And that remains the case.”

Bawazir warned it would be a mistake to accept assurances from a group that is “connected to a deviant state in the region,” referring to Iran, as it may be seen as legitimizing the Houthis. But he said Yemen was comfortable with the U.S. position.
“We do indeed discuss this particular issue very, very deeply,” he said.

title: Trump welcomes Xi for a White House summit set to be high on pageantry, low on substance
summary: Both the U.S. and Chinese leaders are seeking to maintain stability in ties between the world’s two biggest economies, with few concrete results expected from their White House meeting.
story: HONG KONG — President Donald Trump’s strong rapport with Xi Jinping is set to be on display in Washington this week as the Chinese leader makes his first U.S. state visit in more than a decade. But below the surface-level pageantry at the White House, little is likely to be resolved as the world’s two biggest economies continue to spar over trade, Taiwan, AI and more.

Since a trade war shook the global economy last year, U.S.-China relations have been at an effective standstill, experts say, buying both sides time to reinforce their strengths and address their vulnerabilities.

Trump, who usually meets with foreign leaders at the White House, was at the tarmac to greet Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, when they arrived at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, outside Washington on Wednesday.

Trump will be greeting Xi in a weaker position than when they last met four months ago, said Allen Carlson, an associate professor of government at Cornell University, as he faces mounting inflation, falling approval ratings, an unpopular war with Iran and a potentially disastrous midterm election result for his Republican Party.

title: U.S. says China trade truce extended by 2 months
summary: The agreement extends the suspension of some tariffs as Chinese President Xi Jinping arrives in Washington for a state visit.
story: The United States and China have agreed to extend a bilateral trade truce that was set to expire in November through Jan. 10, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Wednesday.
The announcement came after Bessent and China’s vice premier, He Lifeng, held an unscheduled meeting in Washington.

“We will extend what we call the ‘Busan Agreement’ — the economic détente between the two countries that was scheduled to end on Nov. 10 — that is going to be extended until Jan. 10,” Bessent said in an interview on Fox News Channel.
Bessent said it’s possible a larger economic package will be agreed upon by January. But it’s also possible to “just roll the current deal” and extend it further.
Trump welcomes Xi at Joint Base Andrews

“There are some deliverables that have not been perfect on the Chinese side, so we also want to see, now that we’ve sat down and told them our expectations, if over the coming months they can be more fulsome in enacting the agreement,” he said.
The announcement, a big win for economic stability in both countries, came only minutes after Chinese President Xi Jinping touched down to begin a multiday state visit to Washington.

Bessent also indicated that there could be further announcements in coming days from the Chinese delegation, including agreements to buy more American agricultural products and potential deals in the financial services sector.
Since Sunday, Bessent and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer have been holding talks with their Chinese counterparts to lay the groundwork for the closely watched state visit.
On Sunday, Bessent and Greer announced that the U.S. and China had proposed exchanging alerts about AI-related hacking incidents, especially those that concern national security.
The U.S. and China could also agree on lists of goods on which lower tariffs would be applied as part of President Donald Trump’s “Board of Trade” initiative with China, Greer told reporters.

“We expect that the types of goods you’ll see in those lists are consumer goods, low-tech items coming in from the Chinese side,” he said. “On the U.S. side, energy products, agricultural goods, potentially medical devices and other things like that.”
Xi’s trip is his first state visit to the U.S. in more than a decade.

News of the trade truce extension is likely to be widely welcomed in Washington and Beijing, given that the U.S. and China are vital sources of goods for each other and for their millions of consumers and businesses.

title: Iran’s president strikes a defiant tone at U.N. after Trump threats
summary: Masoud Pezeshkian’s appearance at the General Assembly was the first time the leader of a country at war with the U.S. has addressed the world body.
story: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian struck a defiant tone during his address at the United Nations General Assembly on Wednesday, the first time the leader of a country at war with the United States has addressed the world body.

“America and Israel attacked us, equipped with the latest technology and weapon systems, and our people stood steadfast,” Pezeshkian said one day after President Donald Trump had threatened to “annihilate” Iran. “Yes, they did hit us, but we did not bend the knee, we did not bow our head.”
Pezeshkian vowed that Iran would not limit its nuclear program, which it maintains is for civilian purposes, while also saying it was open to negotiations.
“Iran’s defense, our defensive systems have been built so that no one can think that bombing of Iranian cities will go unanswered. That is why we have the military power we do for defense,” he added.
Pezeshkian also highlighted civilian casualties by holding up a picture of children killed when a U.S. munition likely hit an elementary school in Minab in southern Iran, NBC News has reported.

While the U.S. military has yet to directly accept the blame for the bombings on the first day of the war, experts commissioned by the U.N.’s top human rights body say they have found “reasonable grounds” to believe America committed war crimes in the strikes, which Iranian state media says killed 168 people, mostly children.
A U.S. representative at the U.N. walked out as Pezeshkian mentioned civilian casualties, and many seats were empty during his address.

Pezeshkian also displayed a photograph of Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, who was killed when the Israeli military targeted his compound in Tehran on Feb. 28, alongside members of his family and senior Iranian officials.

“I don’t know what standing Iran has to lecture anyone on human rights or the international system when they habitually violate it,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters after the speech. “They violate the sovereignty of every one of their neighbors by sponsoring terrorist organizations that reside in the borders of those countries. They slaughter their own people.”
Pezeshkian’s address followed Trump’s speech Tuesday, during which the American president threatened to destroy Iran.

“I have a big decision to make,” Trump said. “Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before, maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East or even the world? Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?”
Despite his threat, Trump later told reporters that U.S. officials had a “very good meeting” with their Iranian counterparts Tuesday.
U.S. envoys held indirect talks with Iranian officials, and Qatari diplomats acted as intermediaries during that meeting, according to a Middle Eastern official with knowledge of the matter.

The Qatari diplomats conveyed questions and responses from U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner to the Iranian officials, who then relayed their answers back via Qatar, the official said.
“I don’t want to mischaracterize this as a major breakthrough, but at the same time I think it was significant that there was at least a conversation,” Rubio said Wednesday.
U.S. delegation walks out of Iranian president's speech
Pezeshkian also noted that further talks could be possible.
“Iran must be understood by Mr. Trump and those who seek to bully us that we are ready for dialogue and diplomacy and negotiations without accepting the language of force,” he said.
Trump also said during his U.N. address that there would likely be a deal with Iran after the U.S. midterm elections in November, though he did not provide any additional details.
Pezeshkian defended Iran’s right to continue with its civilian nuclear program.
“We say it clearly: no nuclear weapons and no limitations to new peaceful nuclear technology,” he said.

Trump has repeatedly said that the goal of attacking Iran was to prevent the development of a nuclear weapon, which Iranian officials have said for years that they are not pursuing. Soon after the war started, however, Iran blocked the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway through which some 20% of the world’s oil flowed before the conflict, sending shock waves through the world economy.
Iran and the U.S. signed a preliminary agreement, often referred to as a memorandum of understanding, in June aimed at ending the war and opening the strait.

But heavy fighting broke out again over the summer, with Iran striking U.S. allies throughout the region. This derailed the talks and left the strait largely closed to maritime traffic as Iran attacked ships and the U.S. imposed a naval blockade, which also included attacks on oil tankers.

The U.S. military announced the death of four American soldiers in July, and Iranian officials have said dozens of civilians have been killed in recent attacks on cities in southern Iran on the coastline of the strait.

Any discussions that take place between American and Iranian officials in New York will likely focus on the opening of the strait, according to Sina Azodi, director of the Middle East studies program at George Washington University.

“The main discussion will be over returning to the MOU, which is essentially lifting the blockade on Iran and Iran lifting the blockade on the Strait of Hormuz,” Azodi said, noting that gas prices have spiked in the U.S., and the Iranian economy has been squeezed by the U.S. naval blockade.

Before traveling to New York, both Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi were under tremendous pressure from Iranian hard-liners not to hold any talks with U.S. officials. Some hard-liners see negotiations with the U.S. as a form of capitulation, and Pezeshkian and Araghchi is likely to face their wrath when they return.
Last year, the late Khamenei set the red lines for Pezeshkian prior to his trip to New York and said negotiating with the U.S. about the country’s nuclear program or other issues would be a dead end.
This year, his son and successor, Mojtaba Khamenei, does not appear to have publicly laid out any parameters for what the Iranian delegation may discuss with their American counterparts.

title: Trump tells U.N. he could ‘annihilate’ Iran but expects a deal after the midterm elections
summary: In a speech to world leaders at the United Nations General Assembly, President Donald Trump defended the Iran conflict and said he was considering whether to “annihilate” the country and drive it “into hell.”
story: In a speech to world leaders at the United Nations General Assembly, President Donald Trump defended the Iran conflict and said he was considering whether to “annihilate” the country and drive it “into hell.”
Or, he said, Iran could make a deal with the U.S. that would allow the nation to rebuild. But that won’t happen until after the midterm elections in November, Trump predicted.
“I believe we’ll make a deal right after the election because it doesn’t make sense for them not to,” Trump said. “They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election.”
Trump later said U.S. envoys met with Iranian officials for three hours on the sidelines of the gathering, an unexpected development that offered a glimpse of diplomatic activity.

But Trump has repeatedly floated new attacks on Iran, even previously threatening death to the entire civilization. On Tuesday, he revived that warning at one of the most prominent platforms for world leaders, with an Iranian delegation in the audience.

“I have a big decision to make,” he said. “Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before, maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East or even the world? Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?”
“Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?” he continued.
Most important, Trump said to applause, is ensuring that “Iran will never have a nuclear weapon.”

Iran’s nuclear potential was “the reality we had to confront,” he argued, and “a reality that far too many preferred to ignore.” Tehran has insisted its nuclear program is for civilian purposes and denied having plans to develop nuclear weapons.
The U.N. assembly comes as the Iran war is about to enter its eighth month.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian is scheduled to address the U.N. on Wednesday. Trump told Fox News that he would “probably” be open to meeting with Pezeshkian but did not announce any specifics.
Add to Google
Add to Google
Trump also highlighted peace deals he has worked on, U.S. actions in the Western Hemisphere and progress on his 20-point peace plan in the Gaza Strip.

Trump’s remarks to the assembly this year come as the U.N.’s Human Rights Council found in a report last week “reasonable grounds to believe” that the U.S. had committed war crimes during “indiscriminate attacks” against an Iranian school and a residential area in February.
The American president traditionally addresses the General Assembly each year.
During his wide-ranging speech, the president said America is “doing better than ever before,” touting the U.S. economy and his approach to immigration and artificial intelligence.
America is ‘leading’
Less than a minute into his remarks, Trump called the U.S. economy “the envy of the world” and pointed to his administration’s tax policy and stock market records.
“Our economy is the envy of the world,” he said. “Our military is the most powerful on Earth. Our technology is second to none, and we are leading in virtually everything.”

Many American voters, though, don’t appear to agree. An NBC News poll conducted in September found that 56% of registered voters disapprove of the job the president is doing, and 55% said they believe his policies hurt the economy.

Gas prices remain high, sitting at an average of $4.47 per gallon, about a 50% increase since the war with Iran began. Diesel prices also spiked, affected by the Iran war as well as the war between Russia and Ukraine. Diesel hit a record $6 per gallon earlier this month before surging higher to $6.52 as of Tuesday, according to AAA.
Later, the president touted his record on immigration, tying his crackdown on the southern border to a drop in violent crime in the U.S.
“The entire world is being lifted by the wealth, strength, spirit and momentum of a newly energized and a very powerful United States of America,” he said.
Plans to ‘encourage’ AI
While Trump declined to endorse guardrails on artificial intelligence, he did push for one change: its name.

Trump said the U.S. would refer in official documents to “superintelligence,” rather than “artificial intelligence.” The word “artificial,” Trump argued, “makes it sound fake, and it is not fake. It’s actually amazing.”
Earlier this month, industry insiders warned that artificial intelligence could lead to human extinction, potentially in the next decade.
Trump said Tuesday that he would not “stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution.”
“We’re going to encourage it, not rein it in,” he said. “We’re going to watch it closely through the Department of Justice.”
Trump has previously said that the only guardrail the U.S. needs is “a STRONG AND SMART” president.
Artificial intelligence is also expected to be a main topic of conversation during Trump’s meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping this week.
Add to Google
Add to Google
Greenland, Ukraine and Venezuela

Trump met with several world leaders on the sidelines of the U.N. gathering, including Venezuela’s interim president, Delcy Rodríguez. It was Rodríguez’s first meeting with Trump since the U.S. captured then-Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, who are in a Brooklyn, New York, jail, awaiting trial.
Weeks ago, Trump said that the U.S. entered an agreement with Venezuela for U.S. majority control of more than 65 billion barrels of oil reserves in Venezuela.
On Tuesday, Trump called it “perhaps the biggest deal ever made,” adding: “To the victor belong the spoils.”

Trump said the Venezuela raid was “proof that the United States will no longer permit threats to America to gain a foothold anywhere in the Western Hemisphere,” noting U.S. attacks on drug cartels before pivoting to Cuba.
“My administration is seeking a fundamental change in the situation in Cuba,” he said, adding, “It will fall.”
In response, the Cuban delegation stood up and left the assembly hall.
Add to Google
Add to Google
Later Tuesday, Trump met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who said: “I hope that we will end this war, and President Trump will help us help us end this war,” Zelenskyy said.
Trump said during his speech that the war in Ukraine would end “more quickly than people understand.”
For years, the president said he would end the war. During his 2024 presidential campaign, he said he could end the war within 24 hours or even before his presidency began.
Last week, Trump signed into law a Russian sanctions bill championed by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C.

He also announced that the U.S. would take over military operations and have “permanent control over security” in Greenland, in a deal signed later Tuesday with the leaders of Greenland and Denmark to try to end the tense standoff over the strategic Arctic territory.

title: Tehran warns of ‘new weapons’ as Trump weighs meeting with Iranian president
summary: Iran warned Monday it would use “new weapons with new capabilities” if the U.S. launched a fresh assault after President Donald Trump ramped up the rhetoric against Tehran over the weekend.
story: Iran warned Monday it would use “new weapons with new capabilities” if the U.S. launched a fresh assault after President Donald Trump ramped up the rhetoric against Tehran over the weekend.

“If a new aggression takes place, we will definitely change the weapons and geography of the war,” Hossein Mohebbi, a spokesman for Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said Monday, according to the semiofficial Fars news agency.
Mohebbi did not provide details on what the new weapons were or which new locations could be hit.

Earlier, Trump said he would “probably” be open to meeting with his Iranian counterpart, President Masoud Pezeshkian, during the United Nations General Assembly this week, Fox News chief foreign correspondent Trey Yingst reported Sunday.

The possibility of a meeting offered a glimmer of hope for a resolution to the nearly seven-month war with Iran, which has resulted in Iran blocking the key Strait of Hormuz, and its Yemeni allies bombing a crucial east-west oil pipeline and threatening another crucial waterway. Resultant economic shock waves have hit the U.S. and the world economy, driving up oil and diesel prices and fueling inflation.

title: U.S. proposes AI alert system with China ahead of Trump-Xi summit
summary: The United States has proposed a new AI safety notification mechanism for President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping to consider at their summit in Washington this week, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday.
story: HONG KONG — The United States has proposed a new AI safety notification mechanism for President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping to consider at their summit in Washington this week, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday, amid global concern over whether the world’s two leading AI powers can work together to contain the technology’s potential dangers.

Speaking to reporters after daylong talks in New York with Chinese officials, Bessent said the two sides had discussed setting up a new U.S.-China AI dialogue that would include a mechanism for alerting each other to AI-related incidents that could affect national security.

“We think that just like with any cross-border activity, that moving from opaque to more transparency between the number one and the number two AI powers in the world is very important,” he said, adding that the two sides had agreed to meet again on the AI issue.
'Godfather of AI': Congress has about a year to get ahead of AI

AI is expected to be high on the agenda when Trump and Xi meet Thursday, especially after warnings from AI leaders in the U.S. that the technology could pose an existential threat within a few years. Trump has dismissed such concerns as a “hoax” while agreeing with AI executives such as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei that the U.S. must not allow China to pull ahead in the global AI race.

Experts caution that the Trump-Xi summit is unlikely to produce any major agreement on AI, citing the high level of distrust between the two countries. China has interpreted calls to slow down AI development as targeted at its own progress.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told reporters that AI talks would not affect U.S. export controls on advanced chips and semiconductor manufacturing equipment that have hindered Chinese AI companies.

Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng and China’s chief trade negotiator, Li Chenggang, did not comment to reporters as they left the talks at JPMorganChase headquarters. A Chinese readout of the talks published by Xinhua, China’s state-run news agency, did not mention the U.S. proposal and said only that the two sides had discussed AI.

Xinhua said the two sides also had “frank, in-depth and constructive exchanges on important economic and trade issues of common concern, including implementing the consensus reached in previous trade consultations and promoting bilateral trade and investment.”
A major question ahead of this week’s summit is whether Trump and Xi will agree to extend a fragile trade truce that is set to expire Nov. 10.

Bessent and Greer said the two sides had agreed to operationalize a new “Board of Trade” that was announced during Trump’s visit to Beijing in May, and were exploring the potential for lower tariffs on “non-sensitive” products.

On the Chinese side, Greer said, those could include consumer goods and low-tech items, while U.S. exports of energy, agricultural goods and medical devices are also being considered. He did not say whether that meant tariffs on those items would be lowered now or that they would only be exempted from fresh duties in the future.

“There is a world where you have a relatively small subset of American and Chinese goods that can be traded in a balanced way that are non-sensitive,” he said. “Then in the future, as trade actions come up, we can consider them as a class unto themselves.”
Jennifer Jett reported from Hong Kong, and Steve Kopack and Allie Canal reported from New York.

title: Three dead in Moscow as Ukraine launches massive drone attack while Russia votes
summary: The largest Ukrainian drone attack reported so far on the Moscow region killed two people ⁠and damaged part of an oil refinery in the capital, authorities said Sunday.
story: Ukraine launched hundreds of drones at Moscow on Sunday, killing two people on the final day of a Russian parliamentary election that President Vladimir Putin has cast as a test of support for the war in ⁠Ukraine.

Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Telegram: “In the Moscow region tonight, our long-range responses hit very noticeably. One of the key enterprises of Russia’s oil industry and an aggressor logistics facility were struck.”
He did not specifically mention the ongoing State Duma election, but added that Moscow could “end its brutal war and choose peace” if there is “political will” to do so.
An oil refinery was damaged in the strike, with videos showing smoke billowing out across the city.
In the village of Sofyino, ‌south of Moscow, a body covered in a stained ‌blanket lay in front of a damaged apartment block, the upper windows of which were blown out.
“Glass went flying, people started screaming and shouting. I turned around and the entrance doors had already been blown out, ⁠debris everywhere,” said resident Vitaliy, who gave only his first name.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said over 1,600 drones had been shot down by Russia since Saturday, including 450 heading toward Moscow.
In a Telegram post, he said: “This unprecedented attack was clearly planned with the aim of disrupting the elections. The enemy did not succeed.”

Moscow region governor Andrey Vorobyov said in a Telegram post that a 74-year-old man in the Orekhovo-Zuyevo District and a 44-year-old woman in Ramenskoye were killed in the attack. A third person later died of their injuries.
He said 15 people were hospitalized, including two teenagers, ages 14 and 15.
In a post on X, Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha said: “My morning today started with congratulations from many foreign colleagues on Moscow Burning Day.”
He added: “Now that the war has come home, Russians have only Putin to blame for it. The message to him is simple: look out the Kremlin window, see the flames over Moscow — and end this war.”
At the same time, Russia continued its strikes on Ukraine, with three children and a woman killed in strikes in the Kyiv region, regional governor Tymur Tkachenko said in a Telegram post.

Kyiv has demonstrated an increasing ability to strike deep inside Russia in recent months, targeting key military and industrial sites as part of an effort to make everyday Russians feel the cost of the war. Russia has hammered Ukrainian cities across the conflict, now in its fifth year.
The State Duma vote, the first since Russia’s full-scale invasion, is expected to see Putin’s United Russia party easily retain ​its ⁠dominance in a process that critics deride as a farce.
The Kremlin is likely to present the outcome as evidence of public backing for Putin’s policies and for the war.

“Participation in the elections is our joint contribution to Russia’s victory,” Putin declared in a video address to the nation days before the vote. It will serve as a reminder that “millions of people are backing our fighters and that we stand together,” he added.

Election authorities say the ⁠three days of voting have proceeded smoothly despite reported cyberattacks on Saturday. Turnout by late morning on Sunday was at over 45% for the ​Duma vote and ⁠regional elections, said Central Election Commission Chairwoman Ella Pamfilova.
Most anti-war ‌candidates have been barred from the ballot.

Anti-war politician Boris Nadezhdin, who tried to challenge Putin in the presidential election two years ago but was barred from running, told NBC News earlier this week that the elections were “crooked” with no trace of real opposition, though he said disapproval could manifest in a higher number of spoiled ballots or increased tactical voting against Putin’s United Russia party.

Figures from the anti-war Yabloko party said they feared for their freedom after courts handed long jail terms to two senior party figures before the ‌vote. Discrediting the army or spreading what authorities regard as fake ‌news is punishable by lengthy prison sentences.
In a small act of defiance, Yabloko’s leader, Nikolai Rybakov, demonstrably spoiled his ballot paper, writing his party’s name and the slogan “For peace.”

“No one in the world can claim anymore that everyone in Russia supports what is happening,” Rybakov told NBC News last week. “Now everyone has seen that millions of people disagree with what’s going on, and they have turned their attention to Yabloko precisely because it consistently advocates for peace and for an alternative to the status quo.”

Russian electoral officials said Saturday that an online voting system in Moscow had come under cyberattack. Kyiv, which has suspended elections under martial law, has dismissed the Russian vote as a “pseudo election.”

Despite what experts see as the election’s predictable outcome, the NEST think tank in Berlin, co-founded by Kremlin critic Mikhail Khodorkovsky, said the vote could ‌still produce awkward moments for the Kremlin at a time of economic strain.

“The consequences of the war are increasingly being felt within the ​country, and accumulated anxiety and frustration may translate into votes for the systemic opposition parties that the Kremlin has allowed to remain on ‌the ballot,” it said in a note.
Initial results are expected to start emerging at around 2 p.m. ET on Sunday, with more complete results available on Monday.

title: Princess Diana’s brother says King Charles ‘gaslit’ him in dispute over book claims
summary: Princess Diana’s brother, Charles Spencer, has accused King Charles of gaslighting him after Buckingham Palace pushed back at his claims about the monarch’s conduct.
story: Princess Diana’s brother, Charles Spencer, has accused King Charles of gaslighting him after Buckingham Palace pushed back at his claims about the monarch’s conduct.

Buckingham Palace released an unusually forceful statement Wednesday ahead of the release of a memoir by Spencer, which charts the breakdown of then-Prince Charles’ marriage to Princess Diana, and the fallout from her death in a Paris car crash in 1997, one year after the royal couple finalized their divorce.

In an initial excerpt released ahead of publication, Spencer recalled a heated phone call with Charles amid a disagreement about funeral arrangements, claiming that a furious Charles had told him Diana would “soon be forgotten.”

“While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and color memory in ways others do not recognize, even many years after such a loss,” the palace had responded.
In an interview with Britain’s Mail on Sunday newspaper, Spencer said: “It is not every day you wake up to find you’ve been gaslit by the king.”
“It was astonishingly provocative and below the belt because it was essentially trying to say I’d lied without the king being able to deny what I’d said,” Spencer added.
“Gaslighting” is a form of manipulation where the manipulator is trying to get someone to question their own reality, memory or perceptions.
In a further interview with the BBC that aired Sunday, Spencer said he told close friends and family at the time about what Charles had said “because it was so monstrous.”
He also appeared to indicate that Charles and Diana’s sons, heir to the throne Prince William and his brother, Prince Harry, were aware of his allegation before the memoir was published.
“I don’t like to talk about what I’ve been speaking about to William and Harry, but this will not be a surprise to them, I will tell you that. These words will not be a surprise to them,” he said.
There has been no public comment from William or Harry on Spencer’s memoir.

Spencer, an earl whose aristocratic family has generational ties with Britain’s royal family, denied that the book, published after years of silence, was motivated by money or score-settling. “I have a duty, as an eyewitness to history, in the final season of my life,” he told the BBC. “I wanted to just put things down that were true.”

He added: “This is not a threat, it’s a fact: I know lots of things about the king which I chose not to include in the book, because they were not relevant. I’m a historian. ... I wanted to give the context.”
Spencer’s book, “Swan Song: Diana, My Sister,” is due to be released publicly on Tuesday.

In other excerpts from the book, published in advance by the Daily Mail newspaper, Spencer writes that Charles sounded “giddily elated” and “like a lottery winner” when they spoke by phone immediately after Diana’s death, adding: “I suspect the prince’s first reaction must have been to think more of how this event might free him to marry the woman he loved, rather than appreciating the loss of one he did not.”
He also speaks about his sister’s mental health and recounts conversations with her, saying she had told him how “things became very difficult indeed in the marriage early on.”

The book also includes an allegation that Diana suspected Charles was “in love with” a member of royal staff during their marriage, separate from his relationship with the now-Queen Camilla, though Spencer says he has no evidence that was true.
Since its initial statement, Buckingham Palace has remained silent on the further allegations in Spencer’s book. The palace again declined to comment Sunday.

Prince Harry, who quit as a working royal six years ago amid a reported rift with senior royals, has remained close to the Spencer family, with his own memoir “Spare” thanking “my mother’s siblings for their love, support, time, and perspective.”

Of his relationship with Harry, Spencer said: “There’s this perception in the media that I’m on Harry’s side. Well, I’m on my deceased sister’s sons’ side, both of them, and if either of them wanted anything, then I’d be equally there for them. I never get involved in one camp or the other, except as a benign figure, I hope.”
The royal family continued to undertake public duties this week even as Spencer’s book has dominated the headlines, with Charles also meeting with senior figures in AI at a summit in Scotland.
